blocks.h: Questions engineering and quality teams ask first

items.q: We don't know yet whether we need distilled or membrane WFI. Where do we start?
items.a: With a route assessment. The limits are the same either way. What decides it is whether your process and loop need hot or ambient WFI, what plant steam and cooling water cost you, whether a market you supply or your corporate standard still calls for distillation, and whether your quality unit is ready to run a membrane control strategy. We write the reasoning down, and we tell you plainly when distillation is the better route.

items.q: Can you supply only one part of the system?
items.a: Yes. Each family is supplied on its own. We design the interfaces, such as the feed limits a still needs or the return temperature a tank sees, so it works with equipment already on your site, including equipment another supplier built.

items.q: Why have one supplier design generation and the loop?
items.a: Because the water is released at the point of use. When generation and distribution are specified separately, the margin between them is nobody's job. If you split the scope, we still write the interface limits into our functional specification and test our side against them at FAT and SAT.

items.q: Where does your scope end and our plant begin?
items.a: We state the battery limits in the proposal and the functional specification, connection by connection: feed water inlet, drains, utilities, network and the point-of-use valves. A typical scope runs from [standard battery limits, e.g. the feed water inlet flange to the point-of-use valve outlets]. Anything outside that line, and who supplies it, is listed so nothing is left between two contracts.

items.q: How do we size generation against storage?
items.a: From your point-of-use demand profile over a full production day. Generation covers the average draw plus sanitization and recovery time, and the tank covers the peaks. We share the calculation with you.

items.q: Do you build to standard platforms or to order?
items.a: [State whether Aquemi offers named standard platforms, their capacity ranges and standard lead time in weeks.] Either way, materials, instrumentation and controls are adapted to your URS, and every system is tested at FAT before it ships.

items.q: Who builds the stills and pure steam generators?
items.a: [State whether stills and pure steam generators are built in-house or by a named manufacturer, and what Aquemi tests and documents]

items.q: Do you supply water systems for laboratories, hospitals or industrial processes?
items.a: The same RO and EDI platform can be built for hospital reprocessing water under CSA Z314, laboratory water under ASTM D1193 and industrial demineralized water. These pages describe the pharmaceutical build; ask for the standard you work to.

items.q: Our system is already running and out of specification. Who do we contact?
items.a: Use the service request page, with the serial number and current readings, for anything out of specification now. For planned changes such as more capacity, new points of use or new controls, see upgrades and retrofits.

facts.l: Hot water sanitization, RO and EDI

blocks.h: Margin at the generator protects the point of use
body: PW is the bulk water for non-parenteral formulation, the final rinse of most cleaning cycles and the feed to Water for Injection (WFI) stills and Pure Steam generators. USP and Ph. Eur. apply their limits at the point of use, after storage and distribution have had their effect.

So the generator's job is margin. Carbon dioxide (CO₂) taken up through a tank vent raises conductivity. A loop that warms in summer adds microbial risk. We size the skid so its outlet sits well below the limit you release against under the worst feed water of the year, and we show that margin at FAT and again at site acceptance testing (SAT).

The same RO and EDI platform can be built for hospital reprocessing water under CSA Z314, laboratory water under ASTM D1193 and industrial demineralized water. This page describes the pharmaceutical build.

blocks.h: Which purification train fits your feed water
rows: Single-pass RO + EDI
Feed is moderate in dissolved solids and alkalinity after softening. PW is the end product.
Fewest stages and lowest energy. Carbon dioxide and silica reach the EDI directly, so CO₂ control is part of the design.
Double-pass RO + EDI
Feed is high in dissolved solids, alkalinity or silica, or the PW also feeds a WFI still or Pure Steam generator with tight feed limits.
Most margin on conductivity, TOC and silica. More pumps and membranes; second-pass concentrate is recycled to the first pass.
Double-pass RO, no EDI
Feed is soft and low in carbon dioxide, and you prefer one membrane technology to maintain.
Least margin against 1.3 µS/cm. pH adjustment between passes is usually needed to hold the limit.
RO + mixed-bed ion exchange
Small or temporary demand, or a bridge while a generator is replaced.
Resin exhaustion, cylinder exchanges and microbial growth in resin beds become deviations to manage. We rarely propose it for new plants.

blocks.h: How water moves through the skid
blocks.caption: Pretreated feed arrives softened and free of chlorine and chloramine. A heat exchanger brings winter feed up to membrane design temperature. The first RO pass removes most dissolved ions, organics, particles and bacteria. Carbon dioxide passes RO as a gas, so we convert it with caustic dosing or strip it with a membrane degasser before it loads the EDI. A second RO pass, where your feed needs one, adds margin on conductivity and silica. EDI polishes the permeate in an electric field, with no acid or caustic regeneration. Water below the conductivity setpoint goes to storage; anything above it diverts until it recovers.

blocks.h: From your feed water analysis to qualified water

items.d: We read your feed water analyses, seasonal temperature range, peak and average demand and your user requirement specification (URS), and ask for what is missing.

Piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs) and general arrangement drawings issued for your review. Product-contact welds logged, inspected and traceable to material heat numbers.

After tie-in we repeat the critical tests on your feed water, then execute IQ and OQ and support the performance qualification (PQ) sampling that follows.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: You are a new supplier. How do we know the skid will pass IQ/OQ on schedule?
items.a: You do not have to take it on trust. Your quality unit approves the FAT protocol before we start. You witness a wet FAT in which every sequence, alarm, interlock and divert runs on water, and you review the executed report and the turnover package before the skid ships. Deviations found at FAT are closed in our shop, not on your site. Ask for the sample turnover package to check the format before you order.

items.q: Can our engineering and QA teams witness the FAT?
items.a: Yes: in person at [test bay location], remotely over [remote witness platform], or both. The FAT and SAT page lists what a remote witness can and cannot see.

items.q: Are the skids registered for pressure and the panels certified?
items.a: Pressure-retaining parts are registered under CSA B51 with a Canadian registration number (CRN) for your province [confirm who registers and for which provinces]. Control panels are built and marked to [panel standard and certification mark held].

items.q: How do you document material traceability and weld quality?
items.a: Every product-contact component is traced to its EN 10204 3.1 certificate by heat number. Every weld has a line in the weld log, tied to the weld map, with [borescope inspection percentage] borescope inspection recorded. The Fabrication page shows each field and what it proves.

items.q: What does FAT prove if the skid runs on your test water, not our feed?
items.a: FAT proves function: every sequence, alarm, interlock and divert, a sanitization cycle reaching temperature at every probe, instrument loop checks and outlet quality on our test water. Performance on your feed water is proven at SAT and OQ. We write the protocols so your quality unit can leverage FAT results in qualification, in line with ASTM E2500 and ISPE commissioning and qualification guidance, where it accepts that approach.

items.q: How do you handle cold feed water in winter?
items.a: RO output falls as water cools. A membrane array rated at 25 °C can lose a third or more of its output at 5 °C, and many Canadian supplies reach that in winter. We size the array at your lowest recorded feed temperature, or add a heat exchanger that holds a design temperature, and we show the capacity at both ends of your range in the mass balance.

items.q: Why EDI instead of mixed-bed ion exchange?
items.a: EDI regenerates continuously in an electric field. There are no acid or caustic deliveries, no regeneration downtime, no resin exhaustion events to investigate and no resin beds for bacteria to colonise between exchanges.

items.q: Single or double pass RO?
items.a: Your feed water decides. High alkalinity, dissolved solids or silica, or a WFI still or Pure Steam generator downstream, point to double pass. Soft, low-alkalinity feed that makes PW only usually suits a single pass ahead of EDI. We show both options against your analysis when the choice is close.

items.q: Our municipal supply is chloraminated. What changes?
items.a: Chloramine must be removed before the RO, because polyamide membranes do not tolerate it. Breaking it releases ammonia. RO rejects ammonium well, but if we raise pH to control carbon dioxide, more of it becomes dissolved ammonia gas, which passes the membrane and reaches the EDI. So we design the chloramine removal and the CO₂ strategy together. Pretreatment covers the removal step.

items.q: Hot water or chemical sanitization?
items.a: Hot water at 80 °C or more leaves no residual to rinse out and test for, and the cycle is proven by temperature at the coldest point. Chemical sanitization suits membranes that are not rated for heat, but adds a residual test to every cycle. Sanitization frequency is set from your trend data during PQ, not fixed at design.

items.q: Can the same skid feed a WFI still or a Pure Steam generator?
items.a: Yes. We size it for your PW draw plus the still or generator feed demand, and design to that equipment's feed limits, typically on conductivity, silica, chloride and total hardness. Those limits go into the functional specification so they are tested at FAT.

items.q: Our feed comes from a private well. Is that a problem?
items.a: Not in itself. USP and Ph. Eur. require PW to be made from water of drinking water quality, so you need to show your well meets it. Iron, manganese, hardness and silica then drive the pretreatment, and we ask for analyses from more than one season because well chemistry moves.

pages.headline: WFI stills sized on your utility costs, with endotoxin margin you can show an inspector
pages.lead: The multi-effect and vapour compression stills we supply make hot Water for Injection (WFI) below the USP <85> bacterial endotoxin limit of 0.25 EU/mL and the USP <645> conductivity limit of 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C. We set the still's endotoxin reduction against your Purified Water (PW) feed, choose the still type on your steam, power and cooling water costs, and ship the factory acceptance test (FAT) report and installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) protocols with it.
pages.primary_cta: Request a still sizing and utility cost proposal

blocks.h: Distillation removes endotoxin by phase change. The margin depends on your feed.
body: WFI is the solvent for parenteral products and the final rinse for product-contact equipment. A still makes it by boiling PW, separating droplets from the vapour and condensing the vapour. Ph. Eur. 0169 asks for exactly that: a still fitted with an effective device to prevent the entrainment of droplets.

A still reduces endotoxin by a fixed factor, not to a fixed level. The FDA Guide to Inspections of High Purity Water Systems notes that many still fabricators guarantee only a 2.5 to 3 log reduction, and describes stills that periodically produced WFI above 0.25 EU/mL because their feed was not treated well enough. So we design the still and the PW system that feeds it as one: the guaranteed reduction factor sets the endotoxin target for your PW, and both go into the functional specification.

Distillation also delivers WFI hot. EU GMP Annex 1 (2022), adopted by Health Canada as GUI-0119 and in force since 1 April 2024, gives constant circulation above 70 °C as an example of storage and distribution that minimizes microbial growth. A still fills a hot loop without reheating.

blocks.h: How a multi-effect still works
blocks.caption: PW is preheated by the distillate and fed to the first column, where plant steam boils it. The pure vapour from each column, after droplet separation, heats the next column and condenses there as WFI. Vapour from the last column condenses in a cooling-water condenser. Concentrated feed carrying the rejected endotoxin and solids leaves to drain from the last column. Distillate below the conductivity setpoint and above the temperature setpoint goes to storage; anything else diverts to drain.

blocks.h: How a vapour compression still works
blocks.caption: Feed water boils in the evaporator. The vapour passes a droplet separator, then a compressor raises its pressure and temperature so it can condense on the other side of the same heat transfer surface, boiling more feed as it does. The condensed WFI and the blowdown preheat incoming feed. Plant steam or electric heaters bring the still to temperature at start-up; after that the compressor supplies most of the energy, and little or no cooling water is needed.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: You are a new supplier. How do we check still fabrication quality before we order?
items.a: Ask for the sample turnover package. It shows the fabrication dossier format: weld map, weld log, borescope records, material certificates by heat number and the pressure vessel documents. Your QA team can audit [the shop that builds the still] and witness its hold points, and your quality unit approves the FAT protocol before we run it.

items.q: Which FAT and turnover documents keep our validation team on schedule?
items.a: The documentation list on this page is what ships with the still. The FAT protocol reaches you [protocol lead time, weeks] before the test for review, the executed report and deviation log before the still ships, and the IQ/OQ protocols with the still, so your team is not writing them during start-up.

items.q: Why distil when Ph. Eur. now allows membrane WFI?
items.a: Since April 2017, Ph. Eur. 0169 accepts reverse osmosis coupled with other suitable techniques, and USP has long accepted any process equivalent or superior to distillation. Distillation still makes sense when you want hot WFI for a hot loop, when your contamination control strategy relies on the longest inspection record, or when steam or cheap power is on hand. Membrane WFI saves energy where ambient storage suits your process. We model both on your data when the choice is close.

items.q: How much endotoxin reduction can we count on?
items.a: Only what the still manufacturer guarantees, which FDA's inspection guide puts at 2.5 to 3 log for many stills. A 3 log still fed at 250 EU/mL would deliver WFI at the 0.25 EU/mL limit, with no margin. So we set an endotoxin target for the PW feed well below that, and design the PW system and its sanitization to hold it.

items.q: What feed water does the still need?
items.a: PW for a multi-effect still, plus the manufacturer's limits on silica and hardness, which scale hot surfaces, and on chloride, which attacks stainless steel at still temperatures. Vapour compression stills often accept softened or RO feed. We write the feed limits into the functional specification and size the PW skid to meet them.

items.q: Does an imported still need a Canadian registration number?
items.a: Yes. Pressure vessels and fittings installed in Canada need a CRN under CSA B51 from the province of installation, and a still designed for another market may need design changes before it is accepted. We include registration in the project schedule from the start. [Confirm Aquemi's CRN process and the provinces covered.]

items.q: What happens at start-up and shutdown?
items.a: Every start-up diverts distillate to drain until conductivity and temperature reach setpoint. The condenser and distillate line drain on shutdown. FDA's inspection guide describes a still whose condenser held about 50 litres of WFI for up to several days between runs, a source of endotoxin; we design so that cannot happen.

items.q: Can the still feed a hot loop directly?
items.a: Yes. Distillate leaves hot and fills a tank and loop circulating above 70 °C, the example Annex 1 paragraph 6.10 gives. Users who need cooler WFI draw it through point-of-use coolers. Storage and distribution covers the loop design.

items.q: Do hot WFI systems rouge, and who deals with it?
items.a: Hot WFI and pure steam systems develop rouge, an iron oxide film on stainless steel, over time. We record the surface condition at handover and include inspection in the service plan, with derouging and repassivation when trends call for it.

pages.title: Membrane WFI: RO, EDI and ultrafiltration | Aquemi
pages.meta: Water for Injection by RO, EDI and ultrafiltration, as Ph. Eur. 0169 allows since 2017: < 0.25 EU/mL endotoxin, a written control strategy, ambient.
pages.eyebrow: WATER FOR INJECTION · MEMBRANE · PH. EUR. 0169 · USP · EU GMP ANNEX 1
pages.headline: Water for Injection by membrane, with the control strategy and validation package your inspector will ask for
pages.lead: Our double-pass reverse osmosis (RO), electrodeionization (EDI) and ultrafiltration (UF) skids make Water for Injection (WFI) at ambient temperature, below the USP <85> bacterial endotoxin limit of 0.25 EU/mL and the USP <645> conductivity limit of 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C, with no plant steam for generation. We design the biofilm and endotoxin controls the EMA expects from a non-distillation system into the skid, and tell you plainly when distillation is the better route.

blocks.h: The limits are the same as distilled WFI. The evidence you owe is not.
body: USP defines WFI as water purified by distillation or by a process equivalent or superior to distillation in removing chemicals and microorganisms. Since 1 April 2017, Ph. Eur. 0169 also accepts a purification process equivalent to distillation: reverse osmosis, single-pass or double-pass, coupled with other appropriate techniques such as EDI, ultrafiltration or nanofiltration. EU GMP Annex 1 (2022), adopted by Health Canada as GUI-0119, repeats that wording in paragraph 6.10.

Conductivity, Total Organic Carbon (TOC), endotoxin and microbial limits do not change with the route. What changes is the burden of proof. A still removes endotoxin by phase change at high temperature. A membrane system runs at ambient temperature, which the EMA's 2017 questions and answers on non-distillation WFI (EMA/INS/GMP/443117/2017) call an ideal environment for biofilm. So the EMA expects a documented control strategy, developed alongside the design, that shows how the system prevents, detects and removes microbial growth and endotoxin.

Ph. Eur. 0169 also asks that notice is given to the manufacturer's GMP supervisory authority before a membrane WFI system is implemented. USP has no such step. We build the system and the evidence together, so the control strategy, the qualification plan and the notice your regulatory team files draw on the same documents.

blocks.h: How water moves through the skid
blocks.caption: Pretreatment delivers feed that is softened and free of chlorine and chloramine, checked by an oxidant sensor before the first RO pass. Two RO passes in series remove dissolved ions, organics, bacteria and endotoxin. Carbon dioxide passes RO as a gas, so we convert or strip it between the passes before it loads the EDI. EDI polishes conductivity with no regeneration chemicals. The final UF membrane is the last barrier to endotoxin and bacteria. Water below the conductivity and TOC setpoints goes to storage; anything else recirculates or diverts until it recovers. The whole train is hot water sanitized on a schedule set from your data.

blocks.h: From route decision to qualified WFI

items.d: We read your WFI demand, feed water analyses, utility costs, storage temperature and the pharmacopoeias and markets you release into, then recommend membrane or distillation in writing, with the reasons.

Risks, design controls, sanitization, monitoring and maintenance written into a control strategy input and a functional specification you approve. These are the documents your notice to the authority draws on.

The skid runs in our test bay against a protocol you approve: sequences, alarms, oxidant and divert interlocks, a full hot water sanitization cycle, UF integrity test and outlet quality.
After tie-in we repeat the critical tests on your feed water, then execute installation and operational qualification (IQ and OQ).

An initial phase with daily sampling at every point, then a year of data to capture seasonal feed changes, as the EMA questions and answers describe. We write the sampling plan with your validation team and support the sampling.

blocks.h: Questions validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Without published plant case studies, how do you show the skid controls microbes and endotoxin?
items.a: With the control strategy on this page, risk by risk, and the evidence behind each line: online total organic carbon (TOC) and conductivity, [ultrafiltration integrity test method and frequency], sanitization proven by temperature at the coldest point, and endotoxin results from FAT and SAT sampling. You review the protocols before FAT, and the sample turnover package shows the format.

items.q: Will you support us during the regulatory notification and inspections?
items.a: We supply the design basis, the control strategy and the qualification data your notification and inspection file need. [Confirm: whether Aquemi engineers attend inspections or answer inspector questions, and on what terms.]

items.q: Will Health Canada and the FDA accept membrane WFI?
items.a: Both inspect against the pharmacopoeia you release to, and USP has allowed WFI by any process equivalent or superior to distillation for many years. Health Canada recognizes USP and Ph. Eur. as Schedule B publications, and its GUI-0119 adopts Annex 1, which names RO coupled with EDI, UF or nanofiltration. Acceptance rests on your data: a sound design, a documented control strategy and a PQ that covers seasonal feed changes.

items.q: Who do we notify, and when?
items.a: Ph. Eur. 0169 asks that notice is given to the manufacturer's GMP supervisory authority before implementation. The EMA questions and answers say that for a site outside the EU it is the authority of the EU importer's Member State, or, where a mutual recognition agreement covers the product, the site's own authority. Your regulatory team confirms which applies to your products and files the notice; we supply the design and control strategy documents behind it.

items.q: Is membrane WFI as safe on endotoxin as a still?
items.a: It can meet the same limit, by a different mechanism. A still relies on one phase change; a membrane system relies on several barriers in series and on keeping them intact and clean. That is why we trend rejection and differential pressure, integrity test the UF, and sample endotoxin after the UF throughout PQ. If your feed carries a high or variable endotoxin load, we say so and model distillation too.

items.q: How long does qualification take?
items.a: Longer than many teams plan for. The EMA questions and answers describe daily sampling at all points in the initial phase, then performance shown over an extended period, typically a year. Most plants start using the water once the initial phase is complete, on a decision their quality unit documents. Build that year into the project schedule from the start.

items.q: Can we store membrane WFI hot?
items.a: Yes. Annex 1 gives circulation above 70 °C as an example of storage that minimizes microbial growth, not a requirement. Heating ambient WFI to fill a hot loop gives back much of the energy saving, so most membrane WFI plants use an ozonated or regularly sanitized ambient loop instead. Storage and distribution covers both.

items.q: How much energy will we save?
items.a: It depends on your steam cost, power cost, demand profile and storage temperature, so we calculate it for your plant rather than quote a percentage. The route assessment shows energy, water to drain, consumables and membrane replacement per cubic metre of WFI for both routes. [Add Aquemi design figures per cubic metre once validated on a delivered system.]

items.q: Can our corporate standard or export markets rule membrane WFI out?
items.a: They can. Some corporate water standards and some national pharmacopoeias still call for distillation. Check every market you release product into before you choose the route. We include that check in the route assessment.

items.q: Have you delivered membrane WFI before?
items.a: [State the number of membrane WFI systems Aquemi has delivered and their status, or state plainly what PW and membrane experience this design builds on.]

items.q: Who services the skid after handover?
items.a: Our service team, from [service locations]. RO and UF membranes, EDI modules and seal kits for your skid are stocked in [stocking location], and a service plan gives you a stated response time of [response time, hours]. Every visit, sanitization check and membrane change ends with a signed report your quality unit can file.

pages.eyebrow: PURE STEAM · EU GMP ANNEX 1 · EN 285 · USP
pages.headline: Pure steam that passes EN 285 dryness, superheat and non-condensable gas tests at the sterilizer
pages.lead: Our pure steam generators supply autoclaves and steam-in-place (SIP) with steam whose condensate meets Water for Injection (WFI) limits, as EU GMP Annex 1 paragraph 6.17 requires, and whose non-condensable gases (no more than 3.5 mL per 100 mL of condensate), dryness and superheat meet EN 285 where the steam is used. We size the generator and the distribution header as one system, because most steam quality failures start in the pipework, and we hand over the test records your validation team needs.
pages.primary_cta: Submit your steam demand for a sizing proposal

blocks.h: Pure steam is qualified on two sets of tests, and only one is about the generator
body: Pure steam sterilizes product-contact surfaces directly: porous and hard-goods loads in autoclaves, vessels and transfer lines by SIP, and stoppers in processors. EU GMP Annex 1 (2022), adopted by Health Canada as GUI-0119 and in force since 1 April 2024, sets two requirements for it in paragraph 6.17. The condensate must meet the current WFI monograph of the relevant pharmacopoeia, with microbial testing not mandatory. And the steam must be assessed periodically for non-condensable gases, dryness value and superheat against validated parameters.

The first set is chemistry. USP Pure Steam tests the condensate for total organic carbon (TOC), conductivity and, where the steam is used to make parenterals, bacterial endotoxin below 0.25 EU/mL. The generator controls these: droplet separation keeps feed water and its endotoxin out of the steam, and feed degassing keeps dissolved carbon dioxide (CO₂) from raising conductivity.

The second set is physics, and EN 285 gives the acceptance criteria most sterilizer manufacturers and inspectors use. These tests are made at the sterilizer. A generator that delivers dry, gas-free steam at its outlet can still fail them at the point of use if the header collects condensate, leaks air in during shutdown, or reduces pressure in one large step. So we design, test and document the generator and its distribution together.

blocks.h: How a pure steam generator works
blocks.caption: PW is preheated and vented, so dissolved air and CO₂ leave before evaporation. Plant steam or electric heaters boil it in the evaporator, on the far side of a double tube sheet. The vapour rises through a separation stage that returns droplets, and the endotoxin and solids they carry, to the evaporator. Pure steam leaves at a controlled pressure, through a sample cooler, to a drained and insulated header. Blowdown removes the concentrated feed.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: You are a new firm. How do you back your FAT and SAT results without an installed base?
items.a: With evidence you can check rather than references: a FAT protocol your quality unit approves, a witnessed test on steam, test instruments with calibration certificates in the report and the raw readings in the executed protocol. At SAT we test steam quality at the sterilizer, where EN 285 is judged, not only at the generator.

items.q: What happens if our steam fails EN 285 at the sterilizer during commissioning?
items.a: We size the generator and the header together, so a header problem is ours to find. We check traps, separators, slope, insulation and pressure reduction, correct them and test again. [Confirm commissioning scope: header correction and retest included or quoted separately.]

items.q: Our sterilizer fails the dryness test. Is it the generator?
items.a: Usually it is the header. Condensate that collects in flat or sagging runs, missing or failed traps, damaged insulation and dead legs all produce wet steam at the sterilizer from a generator that tests dry at its outlet. We survey the header and the generator together, test at the generator and at the sterilizer, and the difference tells you where the water comes from.

items.q: Does the condensate really have to meet WFI?
items.a: For steam that sterilizes materials or product-contact surfaces directly, yes: Annex 1 paragraph 6.17 asks for condensate that meets the current WFI monograph, without microbial testing. USP Pure Steam applies its 0.25 EU/mL endotoxin limit when the steam is used to make parenterals. Steam that only heats jackets or coils, without product contact, can be plant steam; your contamination control strategy should say which users are which.

items.q: EN 285 is a European sterilizer standard. Does it apply to us?
items.a: EN 285 is written for large steam sterilizers, and its steam quality clause gives the acceptance criteria for gases, dryness and superheat. Annex 1, which Health Canada applies as GUI-0119, names the same three parameters but sets no numbers, so most sites and sterilizer manufacturers use the EN 285 values. If your sterilizer manufacturer specifies different limits, we design to the stricter of the two.

items.q: How often do we have to test?
items.a: Annex 1 asks for a sampling schedule that obtains representative steam regularly and for periodic assessment of the physical parameters. It sets no interval. A common approach is condensate chemistry and endotoxin quarterly, non-condensable gases quarterly until the data support a longer interval, dryness annually, and superheat watched continuously from pressure and temperature. Your validation plan sets the actual frequency.

items.q: What feed water does the generator need?
items.a: USP allows pure steam to be made from drinking water, but feed impurities concentrate in the evaporator. Silica and hardness scale the heat transfer surface, chloride attacks stainless steel at these temperatures, and CO₂ and ammonia raise condensate conductivity. We feed from PW or RO permeate and write the feed limits into the functional specification, so blowdown and cleaning intervals are predictable.

items.q: Where does superheat come from?
items.a: Mostly from reducing the pressure of dry saturated steam in one large step, or through a small orifice close to the sterilizer. Superheated steam behaves like hot air until it cools to saturation, so sterilization is less effective. We stage pressure reduction and place it far enough upstream for the steam to return to saturation before the sterilizer.

items.q: Can we use our WFI still instead of a separate generator?
items.a: Often, yes. The first column of a multi-effect still can deliver pure steam, with WFI output reduced while it does. It suits small or intermittent steam demand. A separate generator is the better choice when sterilizers and SIP run while WFI demand is high, or when you want to maintain one without stopping the other.

items.q: Does an imported generator need a Canadian registration number?

We include registration in the project schedule from the start. [Confirm Aquemi's CRN process and the provinces covered.]

pages.title: PW and WFI storage and distribution loops | Aquemi
pages.meta: PW and WFI loops with turbulent flow per EU GMP Annex 1, dead legs to ASME BPE L/D ≤ 2, full drainage, and hot, ozone or heat sanitization.
pages.eyebrow: STORAGE AND DISTRIBUTION · EU GMP ANNEX 1 · ASME BPE
pages.headline: Storage and distribution loops that keep turbulent flow and compendial quality to the furthest point of use
pages.lead: We design and build tanks and loops for Purified Water (PW) and Water for Injection (WFI) that keep flow turbulent at peak draw, as EU GMP Annex 1 paragraph 6.9 requires, hold every branch to the ASME BPE dead leg target of a length-to-diameter ratio (L/D) of 2 or less and drain completely. Hot WFI loops circulate above 70 °C (Annex 1, 6.10); ambient loops are sanitized by heat or ozone on a schedule you can defend. Every slope, weld and branch is recorded on the as-built isometrics your validation team qualifies against.
pages.primary_cta: Send your points-of-use list for a loop review

facts.l: Loop return velocity at peak draw

blocks.h: Water is released at the point of use. That is where the loop is judged.
body: USP and Ph. Eur. apply their PW and WFI limits to water as it is used, after it has sat in a tank and travelled through tens or hundreds of metres of pipe. A generator that makes water well below the limit gives you margin. The storage and distribution system decides how much of that margin reaches the furthest valve.

Most microbial excursions that trace back to the loop have the same short list of causes: a branch that holds still water, a run that does not drain, flow that drops to laminar when several valves open at once, a wet vent filter, or a sanitization cycle that never reaches the coldest point. EU GMP Annex 1, which Health Canada applies as GUI-0119, names most of them directly: drainable slopes and no dead legs (6.7), turbulent flow that is monitored (6.9), heated and integrity-tested vent filters (6.11) and sanitization on a predetermined schedule (6.12).
We design against each of those causes, then record the evidence on drawings and test reports, so the question an inspector asks about any branch has an answer on paper.

blocks.note: Values in brackets are set for your loop in the functional specification and confirmed by hydraulic calculation. Velocity and Reynolds number targets are design practice, not compendial limits; Annex 1 asks for turbulent flow, established at qualification and monitored.

rows: Counts high at one point of use
A dead leg, an outlet used rarely, or a hose left attached and wet

Temperature mapping of a full sanitization cycle at SAT and operational qualification (OQ)
Ozone at the point of use
UV lamp failure or a dose too low for the flow
UV intensity monitoring, ozone sensor after the UV interlocked to stop supply
Interlock tests in the factory acceptance test (FAT) and OQ protocols; residual ozone test after each loop sanitization
Rouge on wetted surfaces
Heat, chloride residues from construction or cleaning, pump erosion, iron carried in from a still
Controlled finish, passivation after fabrication, chloride-free test water, inspection points at the tank and pump
Passivation and finish reports; inspection points you can trend

blocks.h: Hot, ambient, ozonated or cold: choosing the microbial control
rows: Hot, above 70 °C
Continuous temperature; the FDA inspection guide calls hot 65–80 °C systems self-sanitizing
Hot WFI from a still; the example Annex 1, 6.10 gives
Simplest to defend. Insulated piping, energy to hold temperature, point-of-use coolers for ambient users, and the highest rouge risk.
Ambient, periodic heat
Hot water sanitization of tank and loop on a predetermined schedule, temperature proven at the coldest probe
PW, and WFI from membrane where your contamination control strategy (CCS) justifies ambient storage
Lower running energy. The loop is out of use during heat-up, hold and cool-down, and heat cycles still drive rouge.
Ambient, ozonated
Dissolved ozone held in the tank; UV destroys it before the loop supply; UV switched off on a schedule so ozone sanitizes the whole loop to the point-of-use valves
PW and membrane WFI where heat cycles are unwanted

No heat cycles, and the tank and piping need not be rated or insulated for heat. Ozone must be measured at three points, proven absent at the point of use before release, vented safely and matched to ozone-compatible seals.
Cold, chilled
Low temperature slows growth but does not kill; periodic heat or ozone sanitization does
Processes that need chilled water at the point of use
Chiller load, condensation on piping and longer sanitization cycles. Choose it for the process, not for microbial control.

blocks.h: How a loop works
blocks.caption: Water from the generator enters a tank fitted with a heated hydrophobic vent filter. A variable speed pump drives it through a heat exchanger that holds loop temperature, or through a 254 nm UV unit that destroys ozone on an ambient ozonated loop, then past every point of use on a continuously sloped main. Water not drawn passes conductivity, temperature, flow and TOC sensors on the return and re-enters the tank through a spray ball, so the head space stays wet and the flow never stops. Points of use that need cooler water are served by a cooled sub-loop or a point-of-use cooler that flushes to drain before use.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: Does a WFI loop have to be hot?
items.a: Not by rule. Annex 1 paragraph 6.10 gives constant circulation above 70 °C as an example of storage that minimizes microbial growth, not the only acceptable method. Ambient WFI loops with ozone or periodic heat sanitization are in use, but your contamination control strategy has to justify the choice and your monitoring data has to support it. Where a still delivers hot WFI, a hot loop is usually the simplest to defend; with membrane WFI, the energy case often favours ambient storage. We set out both for your demand.

items.q: Which L/D do you design to, and how do you measure it?
items.a: L/D ≤ 2, the ASME BPE target: L from the inside wall of the main pipe to the valve seal point, D the inside diameter of the branch. It applies to instrument tees and sample valves as well as points of use. The older six-diameter rule comes from the FDA's 1993 inspection guide, which notes it was developed for hot 75–80 °C systems; we do not design to it. Every branch is listed with its L/D in the dead leg register.

items.q: How do you keep flow turbulent when several points of use open at once?
items.a: We take the worst-case combination of outlets from your survey, not the average, and size the pipe and pump so the return stays turbulent with all of them open. A variable speed pump holds return flow or pressure as demand changes, and a low-return-flow alarm tells you when it cannot. At SAT we open the worst-case outlets together and record the return flow, which gives you the qualified flow rate Annex 1, 6.9 asks you to monitor.

items.q: Ozone or periodic heat for an ambient PW loop?
items.a: Ozone keeps the tank under continuous control and sanitizes the loop without heat cycles or insulated piping, at the cost of ozone and UV monitoring, ozone-compatible seals and an extra test after each sanitization. Periodic heat needs no residual test but takes the loop out of use for each cycle and needs heating capacity. Your utilities, your tolerance for downtime and any existing equipment usually decide it; we show both against your schedule.

items.q: How do you prove there is no ozone at the point of use?
items.a: An ozone sensor after the UV destruct unit is interlocked to stop supply if ozone breaks through, and the UV intensity is monitored. After each loop sanitization the water is tested for residual ozone before the loop returns to use, in line with Annex 1, 6.12, which asks for water to be tested after disinfection. The interlock is tested at FAT and OQ.

items.q: How should points of use be sampled?
items.a: The way the water is used. The FDA inspection guide says that if a hose is usually attached, the sample should be taken at the end of the hose, and flush times should match production practice. Annex 1, 6.13 asks for a sampling programme that covers all outlets and points of use at a specified interval, with at least one representative sample every day of water used in manufacturing. We place sample valves for the return and the tank, and write point-of-use sampling into the PQ protocol.

items.q: What about rouge?
items.a: Rouge, the iron oxide film that forms on stainless steel, is found mainly in hot WFI and pure steam systems and in systems with frequent heat cycles. On its own it does not usually move conductivity or TOC, but loose rouge that migrates is a particle risk, and your quality unit will expect it to be inspected and trended. We limit the causes at design (finish, passivation, chloride control during construction, pump selection), give you inspection points at the tank and pump, and plan derouging and repassivation as maintenance rather than an emergency.

items.q: Can you add points of use to an existing loop?
items.a: Yes, after a hydraulic check of the whole loop at the new peak draw. Each new branch is cut in with a zero-static valve, orbitally welded, passivated and added to the isometrics and dead leg register, under your change control, with a requalification scope agreed before work starts. Shutdown length depends on the tie-ins: [typical shutdown for a point-of-use addition, days]. See upgrades and requalification.

items.q: Can the loop connect to a generator from another supplier?
items.a: Yes. We define the interface in the functional specification: water quality and flow at the tank inlet, the signals exchanged, and how a generator divert or a low tank level is handled, so the loop and the generator are qualified as one system.

items.q: How do you document slope, orbital welds and borescope inspection in the turnover package?
items.a: Slope is recorded line by line on the as-built isometric drawings, [slope verification method]. Every weld has a line in the weld log tied to the weld map and the material heat numbers, with [borescope inspection percentage] borescope inspection recorded. The Fabrication page shows each field and what it proves.

items.q: Who services the loop after handover?
items.a: Our service team, from [service locations]. A service plan covers vent filter replacement and integrity tests, instrument calibration, pump seals, UV lamps and rouge inspection, with a stated response time of [response time, hours]. Every visit ends with a signed report your quality unit can file.

pages.title: RO pretreatment for pharmaceutical water systems | Aquemi
pages.meta: Pretreatment that takes drinking water meeting USP <1231> and holds RO feed at no detectable chlorine or chloramine and SDI ≤ 3, in every Canadian season.
pages.eyebrow: PRETREATMENT · USP <1231> · HEALTH CANADA · US EPA NPDWR
pages.headline: Pretreatment that keeps chlorine, chloramine and scale off your RO membranes in every season
pages.lead: USP <1231> requires the feed to a Purified Water (PW) system to meet drinking water standards, such as the US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (NPDWR) or, for most Canadian sites, the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality. Drinking water is not reverse osmosis (RO) feed. We design the pretreatment train from your water data across the seasons, so the RO inlet sees no detectable chlorine or chloramine, a silt density index (SDI) of 3 or less and hardness the membranes can live with, and the carbon bed is sanitized so it does not become the source of your bioburden.

facts.l: Free chlorine and chloramine as Cl₂

blocks.h: Drinking water standards protect people, not membranes
body: Every pharmacopoeial water starts as drinking water. USP <1231> sets the NPDWR, or equivalent EU, Japanese or WHO drinking water rules, as the minimum quality of the source. Ph. Eur. asks for water intended for human consumption. In Canada your municipality treats to the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality and its provincial regulation. Meeting that standard is your starting point and, for a private well, something you have to show.

Those standards are set for health and taste, and they allow water that damages RO membranes. The NPDWR allows a chloramine residual up to 4 mg/L as Cl₂. Health Canada sets no limit for chloramine at all, because at drinking water levels it is not a health concern. Polyamide RO membranes are typically rated for less than 0.1 mg/L free chlorine. Hardness has no health limit; a few milligrams per litre of calcium in the RO concentrate is enough to scale it.

Pretreatment closes that gap. It also creates a risk of its own: once the carbon removes the disinfectant residual, nothing in the water holds bacteria back. So we design removal and microbial control together, and we monitor the outlet that your validated system depends on.

blocks.h: Canadian feed water: what changes, and what it does to your RO
rows: Chloramine instead of free chlorine
Many large municipal utilities use chloramine as the residual disinfectant in the distribution system. Some switch temporarily to free chlorine for system maintenance.
Oxidizes polyamide RO membranes. Reacts slowly on standard carbon. Breaking it releases ammonia, which can reach the EDI.
Carbon contact time sized for chloramine, catalytic carbon or bisulfite, total chlorine measured at the RO inlet, and an ammonia and CO₂ strategy agreed with the PW skid design.
Cold winters, warm summers
Surface water intakes can fall to near 2 °C in winter and pass 20 °C in late summer.
Cold water cuts RO output and lowers silica and calcium solubility. Warm water speeds bacterial growth in carbon beds and softeners.
Membranes sized at your coldest month or a feed heat exchanger, scaling checked at both ends of the range, sanitization frequency set for summer.
Spring runoff and fall turnover
Rivers and lakes carry more turbidity, colour and natural organic matter in the freshet and when lakes turn over.
Higher SDI and total organic carbon (TOC) foul membranes and load the carbon. TOC at the RO inlet moves TOC at the PW outlet.
Media filter sized for the worst month, SDI tested on site, ultrafiltration where SDI cannot be held by media alone.
Hardness and alkalinity
Great Lakes water is moderately hard. Many groundwaters in Ontario, the Prairies and Quebec are much harder.
Calcium carbonate scales the last RO elements. Alkalinity becomes carbon dioxide that loads the EDI.
Duplex softeners regenerated on measured hardness, concentrate Langelier saturation index (LSI) checked, alkalinity handed to the PW skid's CO₂ removal.
Silica
Higher in groundwater and some prairie and Shield-region surface water.
Silica passes softeners. It scales RO concentrate, limits recovery and loads the EDI and any still downstream.
Recovery limited by silica at your coldest feed, antiscalant where projections need it, and silica in the feed limits of the WFI still or Pure Steam generator.
Iron and manganese
Mostly well water, sometimes in older municipal mains. Health Canada sets an aesthetic objective of 0.1 mg/L for iron and a maximum acceptable concentration of 0.12 mg/L for manganese.
Oxidized iron and manganese foul membranes and coat softener resin, often at levels drinking water allows.
Oxidation and catalytic media filtration ahead of the softener, sized on analyses from more than one season.
No disinfectant residual after carbon
Every dechlorinated train, worst in summer and after low-flow weekends.
Carbon beds and softeners grow biofilm that sheds into the RO and raises bioburden in PW.
Hot water sanitizable carbon, sampling before and after each bed, and continuous flow or recirculation at no demand.

blocks.h: Chlorine or chloramine: choosing the removal step
rows: Granular activated carbon
Free chlorine within a few minutes of contact. Chloramine only slowly.
No chemicals. Also removes some organics.
Biofilm in the bed once the residual is gone. Needs hot water or steam sanitization, backwashing and planned media replacement.
Catalytic carbon
Free chlorine and chloramine, with less contact time than standard carbon.
The usual choice where the utility chloraminates.
Same microbial control as any carbon bed. Bed volume is set by empty bed contact time at peak flow and your winter temperature, when the reaction is slowest.
Two carbon beds in series
Free chlorine and chloramine, with a second bed that catches breakthrough from the first.
Sample point between beds shows breakthrough before it reaches the RO. Dialysis water practice (ISO 23500) uses this arrangement for chloraminated supplies.
Two vessels to sanitize and maintain.
Sodium bisulfite dosing
Free chlorine and chloramine, by chemical reduction.
Small footprint, fast response. No carbon bed to colonise.
Dose control and online verification. Overdosing feeds sulfate-reducing bacteria on the membranes. Ammonia from chloramine passes to the RO.
UV dechlorination (high intensity)
Free chlorine and chloramine, by photolysis.
No chemicals and no carbon bed. Also reduces bacteria.
High lamp power at high chlorine levels. Needs low turbidity feed, and a total chlorine analyser downstream because lamp output decays.

blocks.h: Microbial control in carbon beds
rows: Hot water or steam sanitization
USP <1231> names carbon beds as a site of microbial growth, and heat is the control that leaves no residual to rinse out.
Stainless steel vessel, hot water rated media and internals, bed held at [sanitization temperature, °C] for [hold time, minutes], verified at the coldest point of the bed.
Frequency from trend data
Growth rate follows temperature, flow and organics, so a fixed calendar either over- or under-sanitizes.
Starting frequency of [initial sanitization interval, days], reset from counts before and after the bed during qualification.
Backwash and flow
Stagnant beds channel and grow biofilm; low-flow weekends are the usual source of a Monday count.
Automatic backwash on pressure drop or time, and recirculation or a minimum flow when the RO is off.
Media replacement
Exhausted carbon stops removing chloramine and organics before it stops passing water.
Replacement on measured breakthrough or [media replacement interval, months], with media certificates in the maintenance record.
Sampling and UV after the bed
You cannot trend what you do not sample.
Sample valves before and after every bed and softener. A 254 nm UV unit at the carbon outlet where your counts need more margin.

blocks.h: How the train is built
blocks.caption: A backflow preventer and break tank isolate the plant from the supply and give the feed pump a steady suction. A multimedia filter removes particles; on well water an oxidation and catalytic media stage removes iron and manganese first. Duplex softeners exchange calcium and magnesium for sodium, with one vessel in service while the other regenerates. We usually place the softener ahead of the carbon, so the chlorine residual still limits bacterial growth in the resin. Activated carbon, or sodium bisulfite dosing, then removes chlorine and chloramine. Antiscalant is dosed where the membrane projection shows silica or other scaling at your recovery. A 5 µm cartridge filter protects the high-pressure pump and the membranes.

blocks.h: From your water data to a pretreatment design basis

items.d: Your utility's annual water quality reports, your own analyses and, for a well, results from more than one season. We list what is missing and how to sample it.
We check the data against drinking water standards and against the limits of the membranes and stills downstream, and tell you which months set the design.
Membrane projections at your coldest and warmest feed, the treatment train, vessel sizes and contact times, and the RO inlet targets, issued for your approval.
Valve sequences, regeneration, backwash, sanitization and alarms tested at factory acceptance testing (FAT) against a protocol you approve.
At site acceptance testing (SAT) we measure SDI, total chlorine, hardness and temperature at the RO inlet on your feed, and hand over the sampling plan.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: As a new supplier, how do you check your design protects our RO through seasonal swings before we order?
items.a: We ask for [months of history] of utility and site data, find the worst month for each parameter (temperature, turbidity, organics, chlorine or chloramine dose, hardness) and size every bed and the softener against those months. You see the design basis, month by month, before you place the order.

items.q: Is pretreatment inside the turnover package and the validation boundary?
items.a: It is in the turnover package either way: drawings, material certificates, media and resin certificates, calibration certificates, FAT records. Whether it sits inside the validated boundary is your call in the risk assessment; we design and document it so either answer holds up.

items.q: How do you control bioburden in carbon beds without chemical carryover to the RO?
items.a: Carbon beds are sanitized with [hot water or steam, at the temperature and hold time on this page], backwashed on a schedule and replaced at [carbon replacement interval]. No biocide is dosed ahead of the RO, so there is nothing to carry over.

items.q: Is pretreatment part of the validated system?
items.a: It depends on where your risk assessment draws the boundary. Many sites qualify from the RO inlet onward and treat pretreatment as supporting equipment under good engineering practice. Its performance still decides whether the RO meets its limits, so we document it to the same standard, test it at FAT and SAT, and supply installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) protocols where you bring it into scope.

items.q: Do we have to prove our feed water meets drinking water standards?
items.a: USP <1231> expects you to know that it does. For municipal supply, the utility's reports plus your own periodic testing at the plant inlet are the usual evidence. For a private well you are the utility, so you need a sampling programme against the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality or the NPDWR, including microbiological tests. We can propose the parameters and frequency.

items.q: Our municipality uses chloramine. Is standard carbon enough?
items.a: Usually not at a reasonable bed size. Chloramine reacts on carbon far more slowly than free chlorine, and slower still in cold water. We size catalytic carbon or two beds in series on contact time at peak flow and winter temperature, or dose bisulfite, and measure total chlorine at the RO inlet, because a free chlorine analyser does not see chloramine.

items.q: What happens to the ammonia from chloramine?
items.a: Removing chloramine releases ammonia. RO rejects it well as ammonium, but at the higher pH used to control carbon dioxide more of it is dissolved ammonia gas, which passes the membrane and loads the EDI. So the chloramine removal here and the CO₂ strategy on the PW skid are designed together. See Purified Water generation.

items.q: Why do our carbon bed counts spike?
items.a: Carbon removes the disinfectant and adsorbs organics, so it grows biofilm, faster in summer and when flow stops. Counts after the bed that rise between sanitizations usually mean the interval is too long, the bed stagnates at no demand or the media is exhausted. We trend counts before and after the bed and set sanitization from that data.

items.q: Why measure SDI on site rather than from the utility report?
items.a: Utilities report turbidity, not SDI, and SDI depends on what the water picks up between the treatment plant and your tap. ASTM D4189 measures it in 15 minutes at your cartridge filter outlet. We test during the feedwater review where we can, and again at SAT.

items.q: Can we keep our existing pretreatment when we replace the RO?
items.a: Often, if it meets the new RO inlet targets. We review its sizing, media age, sanitization capability and monitoring against your feed data, and tell you what to keep, upgrade or replace. See upgrades and retrofits.

items.q: Our utility switches to free chlorine for a few weeks each year. Does that matter?
items.a: Yes, in both directions. Free chlorine reaches the carbon at a higher oxidant level, and the switch back changes what the bed must remove. Ask your utility for its schedule; we design for both disinfectants and alarm on total chlorine at the RO inlet.

items.a: Our service team, from [service locations], on a plan with a stated response time of [response time, hours]. Media, resin and cartridges for your train are stocked in [stocking location], and every visit ends with a signed report your quality unit can file.

pages.title: Water system monitoring, controls and Part 11 | Aquemi
pages.meta: Online TOC to USP <643>, conductivity to USP <645> stage 1 and audit trails to 21 CFR Part 11 and Annex 11, on PLC and SCADA validated to GAMP 5.
pages.eyebrow: MONITORING AND CONTROLS · USP <643> · USP <645> · 21 CFR PART 11 · GAMP 5
pages.headline: Water quality data you can release on and defend in an inspection
pages.lead: We build the controls and online monitoring for Purified Water (PW) and Water for Injection (WFI) systems so every release decision rests on a record an inspector can trace: total organic carbon (TOC) against the USP <643> limit of 0.50 mg/L on an analyzer with documented system suitability, conductivity against the USP <645> stage 1 table on the raw, non-temperature-compensated reading, and an audit trail that meets 21 CFR Part 11 and EU GMP Annex 11. The software follows the GAMP 5 lifecycle, and the specifications, test records and traceability your validation team needs are written as we build it.

blocks.h: Your water is released on data. The data is what gets inspected.
body: Once online TOC and conductivity are qualified, the numbers they record are the release evidence for every batch that used the water. An inspector reviewing your water system does not stop at the result. They ask for the raw conductivity and temperature behind it, the last TOC system suitability test, who changed an alarm limit and why, which alarms were acknowledged without action, and whether the audit trail has been reviewed.

Data integrity findings in water systems usually come from a small set of gaps: a transmitter that shows only a temperature-compensated value, an operator panel with shared logins, a historian whose clock drifts from the programmable logic controller (PLC), alarm limits changed with no reason recorded, or an audit trail that exists but nobody reviews. The FDA's 2018 questions and answers on data integrity and current good manufacturing practice (CGMP), the PIC/S guidance PI 041-1 and the MHRA's GxP data integrity guidance all address them. Health Canada is a PIC/S member and applies the same expectations.

We design against each of those gaps at the specification stage, test them at factory acceptance testing (FAT), and hand you the evidence, so the controls are something your quality unit can defend rather than something it has to work around.

blocks.h: The temperature-compensation caveat
body: Most conductivity transmitters display a value compensated to 25 °C, because it is easier to trend. USP <645> stage 1 does not use it. The test compares the uncompensated conductivity with the table value for the measured temperature, rounded down to the next 5 °C step. Compensation algorithms are written for ordinary waters, and in ultrapure water at loop temperatures they can move the reading enough to pass water that the compendial test would send to stage 2, or the reverse.

So we record both. The historian stores the raw conductivity and the temperature as the compendial record, and the stage 1 limit is looked up for each reading from the USP table. The compensated value is kept for trending and is labelled as such on every screen and report, so nobody releases on the wrong number.

blocks.h: How the controls are built
blocks.caption: Instruments report to a programmable logic controller (PLC) that runs sequences, interlocks, divert and sanitization, and keeps running if every layer above it fails. Operators work at a local human-machine interface (HMI) with individual logins. A supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) system and historian stores the quality data, the audit trail and the alarm history, with clocks synchronized to one time source. The historian connects to your plant network, building management system or plant historian through a firewall and demilitarized zone (DMZ) segmented in line with ISA/IEC 62443. Remote support, where you choose it, enters only through a connection you open, control and log.

blocks.h: Risk-based testing, not a stack of screenshots
body: GAMP 5 (second edition, 2022) and the FDA's computer software assurance (CSA) guidance for production and quality system software (finalized in 2025, revised in 2026, written for medical device manufacturers and widely applied in pharma), both ask for testing scaled to risk and for the use of supplier testing where it is well documented. We apply that thinking within your validation policy. Functions that touch product quality, such as divert, quality alarms, sanitization temperature and the audit trail, get scripted tests with recorded evidence. Low-risk display functions can be verified with unscripted or exploratory testing.

Because we write and test the PLC code ourselves and run FAT on the full system, your team can leverage the FAT records in OQ instead of repeating them, if your procedures allow it and the protocols are approved before execution. Your validation team approves the strategy and owns the final computerized system validation.

blocks.h: Questions validation, QA and IT teams ask

items.q: How can our QA team check your controls and validation approach without a prior plant audit record?
items.a: Before you order, review the sample FAT protocol and turnover package, the functional and design specifications for your system and the traceability matrix from each requirement to its test. Your QA team can audit [our software development and change control procedure] and witness the controls FAT.

items.q: Do we get full access to the PLC and HMI code, or are we locked in?
items.a: [Confirm: application code delivered unlocked with the turnover package, and who owns it.] The software version and checksum seen at FAT are recorded, so you can show an inspector that the code running is the code that was tested.

items.q: How do you test the controls at FAT before shipment?
items.a: Every input and output is checked, every sequence, alarm and interlock is run on water, and audit trail entries, user access levels and recovery after a power failure are tested against the functional specification. The FAT and SAT page lists each test case and what IQ/OQ can leverage.

items.q: Can you fit new controls to a skid or loop from another manufacturer?
items.a: Yes, as an upgrade: we survey the instruments and valves you keep, write the functional specification against your current qualified state and plan the cut-over and requalification. See Upgrades and retrofits.

items.q: Can we release water on online TOC and conductivity?
items.a: Yes, for those two attributes, when the instruments are qualified, the sample point represents the water used and your procedures say so. USP <643> and <645> both allow online measurement. Online conductivity covers stage 1 only; a stage 1 failure goes to stages 2 and 3 in the laboratory. Microbial counts and, for WFI, bacterial endotoxin stay laboratory tests unless you qualify an alternative method.

items.q: Our transmitters show temperature-compensated conductivity. Is that a problem?
items.a: For trending, no. For USP <645> stage 1, the compendial record must be the uncompensated conductivity with the measured temperature, compared with the table value for that temperature rounded down to the 5 °C step. We configure transmitters and the historian to store both and label which is which. On an existing system, this is one of the first things we check.

items.q: How often does the online TOC analyzer need system suitability?
items.a: USP <643> requires system suitability, with a response efficiency between 85 % and 115 % on the sucrose and 1,4-benzoquinone standards, but does not fix the interval for online instruments. It is set in your procedures, usually after calibration and at a frequency you justify from the analyzer's history. We perform it at SAT and write the procedure into the maintenance manual.

items.q: Is your system Part 11 compliant?
items.a: No system is compliant on its own; your site is, by technical controls in the system plus procedures. We supply the technical controls: audit trail, access control, electronic signatures, record protection and backups. The Part 11 and Annex 11 assessment shows, clause by clause, which controls are in the system and which need a procedure at your site, such as account administration and audit trail review.

items.q: Who validates the software?
items.a: Your validation team approves the strategy and owns the computerized system validation. We supply the specifications, the risk assessment, the traceability matrix and executed FAT, SAT and OQ records written so they can be leveraged under your procedures.

items.q: Can you connect to our plant historian, and where does the Part 11 boundary sit?
items.a: Yes, through OPC UA or another standard protocol. We agree in the functional specification which system holds the original record. If your plant historian is the record, ours buffers data through a network loss so nothing is missing; if ours is the record, yours receives a copy for dashboards.

items.q: Our IT team will not allow remote access to GMP equipment.
items.a: Then we do not install it. The system runs and records fully without any outside connection. If you later allow read-only telemetry or supervised sessions, they connect through your DMZ under your IT and change control, with every session logged.

items.q: Who sets the alert and action levels?
items.a: You do, with our input. At handover there is little data, so we start from your specification and the generator's design margin, then recommend alert levels from qualification data, as Annex 1, 6.13 expects, and reassess them once routine monitoring builds history.

items.q: Can you fix data integrity gaps on an existing water system?
items.a: Yes. We start with a gap assessment against Part 11, Annex 11 and USP <645>: shared logins, missing audit trail, compensated-only conductivity, unsynchronized clocks, paper recorders. Then we propose an upgrade scoped to the gaps, with a requalification plan agreed with your quality unit before work starts. See upgrades and requalification.

items.a: Our service team, from [service locations], with a stated response time of [response time, hours]. A service plan covers calibration, TOC system suitability, UV lamps, ozone sensors, backups and software patches under your change control. Every visit ends with a signed report.

blocks.h: Qualification evidence is lost between suppliers, not inside them
body: Each stage of a water system produces evidence the next one depends on. IQ verifies the installation against the approved P&IDs (Annex 15, 3.9). FAT results stand in for IQ/OQ tests only where the protocol was written to be leveraged and transport and installation cannot affect the function (Annex 15, 3.6). PQ alert levels come from data on a system whose design intent is known. Service keeps that state only if every part fitted and every calibration traces back to the qualified design, and every change goes through change control (Annex 15, section 11).

When four companies hold four sets of documents, your validation team becomes the integrator: reconciling tag numbers, repeating tests already run at the factory because the protocol was not approved in time, rebuilding a dead leg register at IQ. We write each document from the one before it, against the same requirement IDs, and send drafts at each stage so your quality unit reviews as we go rather than at the end.
Each service can also be bought alone. When we join a project part way, we tell you at the start what we need from the parties before us for the record to hold together.

pages.eyebrow: PROCESS DESIGN · URS TO DESIGN QUALIFICATION · EU GMP ANNEX 15 · ASTM E2500 · ICH Q9
pages.headline: Water system design traced to your URS, approved at DQ and built to qualify
pages.lead: EU GMP Annex 15 makes the user requirement specification (URS) the point of reference for the whole validation lifecycle, and asks that design qualification (DQ) verify every one of its requirements. We turn your URS into a basis of design, mass balance, piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs) and a functional specification in which each requirement carries an ID, traced to the drawing that meets it and the test that proves it at factory acceptance testing (FAT), site acceptance testing (SAT) and installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ). A risk assessment to ICH Q9(R1) marks the critical design elements, so qualification effort goes where water quality is decided.
pages.primary_cta: Submit your URS for a gap review

blocks.h: Most qualification problems are designed in, long before the IQ protocol is written
body: A loop sized on an average draw fails turbulent flow at peak. A branch drawn without its length fails the dead leg check at IQ. A divert setpoint that lives only in the programmer's head becomes an OQ deviation. Each of these is cheap to fix on a drawing and expensive to fix in a qualified room.

So we write the design to be checked. Every URS line gets an ID and a written answer: met, met with a condition, or not met and why. The basis of design records each sizing decision with the data behind it. The functional specification states every setpoint, alarm and interlock as a testable sentence. The P&IDs carry the instrument tags and dead leg dimensions the IQ protocol will verify.

That is what Annex 15 (3.2 and 3.3) asks of a URS and a DQ, and what ASTM E2500 and the ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 5 for commissioning and qualification (C&Q) build on: specify from product and process requirements, find the critical aspects by risk assessment, and verify them once, at the point where the evidence is best.

blocks.h: Questions engineering, validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Our URS is a draft. Is it too early to send it?
items.a: No. A draft is the best time. Annex 15, 3.2 says the essential elements of quality should be built in at the URS stage, and the cheapest change is a sentence. We return the compliance matrix with gaps, conflicting requirements and requirements no one could test, each with a proposed wording. The URS stays yours to approve.

items.q: Who owns DQ: you or us?
items.a: You do. Annex 15, 3.3 describes DQ as the documented verification that the design meets GMP and the URS, and the 2025 revision of ASTM E2500 calls for quality unit approval of it. We supply the design review report, the traceability matrix and the risk assessment as evidence, in your template if you have one. Your quality unit decides.

items.q: Can tests at FAT count towards qualification?
items.a: Where it is justified. Annex 15, 3.6 allows documentation review and some tests at FAT without repeating them at IQ/OQ, if you can show transport and installation do not affect the function. We plan which tests qualify for that in the commissioning and qualification plan during detailed design, and write the FAT protocol so your quality unit can review and approve it before execution.

items.q: Our site does not use ASTM E2500. Does that change your design?
items.a: Not the documents. The basis of design, P&IDs, functional specification and risk assessment are the same. What changes is how much is verified, by whom and how often it is repeated. We deliver in the qualification approach your procedures describe.

items.q: Which risk assessment method do you use?
items.a: ICH Q9(R1) does not prescribe one. For water systems we usually run a failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) at component and function level, with your quality and engineering leads in the room, because the people who will operate the system know failure modes a designer misses. We use your template and scoring if your procedures set one. The output is a list of critical aspects and critical design elements, and the verification each needs.

items.q: Can you work with our engineering firm's design?
items.a: Yes. We can design the water system inside a package your architect-engineer leads, with our P&IDs, GA drawings and utility list issued for their drawings, or review a water system design they have produced against your URS and the standards above. [State whether a design-only or design review engagement is sold separately from equipment, and how it is priced.]

items.q: What happens if our requirements change after design freeze?

We state which documents it touches, whether it affects a critical aspect or critical design element, and what has to be re-reviewed or retested, before you decide. Changes that touch no critical element can usually follow the engineering change process, as ASTM E2500 allows.

items.q: Do you design for future capacity?
items.a: Yes, for the expansion you name. We size the loop and tank for it or add capped tie-in points, and state in the basis of design what a later phase would need, so a second phase does not mean a new loop or a new qualification of the whole system.

pages.eyebrow: FABRICATION · ASME BPE · ASME SECTION IX · EN 10204 3.1 · ASTM A967
pages.headline: Fabrication your auditor can trace from any weld back to the mill heat
pages.lead: We build skids, tanks and distribution loops in 316L stainless steel to ASME BPE, with autogenous orbital welds made by welding operators qualified to ASME Section IX. Every product-contact weld is numbered on the isometric and logged with its operator, procedure, weld schedule, sample weld (coupon), inspection result and the EN 10204 3.1 heat numbers of the two parts it joins. Surface finish, passivation to ASTM A967 or ASTM A380, slope and pressure test each leave a signed record, so your supplier audit and your installation qualification (IQ) check documents, not memories.

blocks.h: Fabrication is where qualification evidence is made, or lost for good
body: A weld cannot be re-inspected once the loop is insulated, and a heat number cannot be recovered once the tube is cut and the marking is gone. If the record was not made at the bench, IQ has nothing to verify against, and EU GMP Annex 15, 3.9 expects IQ to check materials and installation against the approved drawings and specifications.

The findings we see in supplier audits are rarely bad welds. They are welds with no inspection record, mill certificates that do not match the heats installed, coupons that were never kept, passivation with no certificate, and slopes that were drawn but never measured. Each one becomes a deviation, a cut-out or an argument with your quality unit.

So our shop works to a written fabrication and inspection plan, agreed with you before the first cut. It names the standard behind each step, the record it produces and the hold points your inspector can witness. The records are filled in as the work is done and handed over as one indexed dossier.
