blocks.h: Questions validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Our specification says 3.1B certificates. Do you supply those?
items.a: 3.1B is the designation from the 1991 edition of EN 10204. The 2004 edition replaced it with 3.1: an inspection certificate with specific test results for the delivered product, validated by an inspection representative independent of manufacturing. We supply 3.1 and can note the equivalence in the material log so your reviewer does not raise it. A type 2.2 test report is not accepted for product-contact parts.

items.q: Which welder qualifications and sample weld procedures do you keep for product-contact tubing?
items.a: Welding procedures are qualified to ASME Section IX with a welding procedure specification (WPS) and procedure qualification record (PQR). Orbital operators hold a welding operator performance qualification (WOPQ); [number of qualified orbital operators]. A sample weld is made at the start of each shift and on any change of operator, power supply, weld head or tube size, examined and kept with the weld log.

items.q: How do you tie 3.1 certificates to the physical tube and fittings?
items.a: Heat numbers are checked against the certificate when material arrives and [how components are marked or tagged]. Each weld log line names the heat numbers on both sides of the weld, so any weld traces back to its certificates.

items.q: Do you borescope every weld?
items.a: Our standard is [share of product-contact welds borescoped, %] of product-contact welds, stated in the fabrication and inspection plan before work starts. ASME BPE allows a random sample; we expect most pharmaceutical customers to specify more. A weld that cannot be reached, such as a final closure weld, is accepted on its coupon and the reason is recorded against its number.

items.q: What happens to a rejected weld?
items.a: It is cut out, not ground or re-fused. The replacement gets a new weld number, its own log line and inspection, and the log keeps the link to the rejected weld so the history is visible. We report the rejection rate in the dossier [state whether the weld rejection rate is reported].

items.q: Can our inspector witness fabrication, and can we audit the shop?
items.a: Yes. Hold and witness points are agreed in the fabrication and inspection plan, typically coupons, borescope review, pressure test and passivation. Supplier audits of the shop and its quality system are welcome before order. [Shop location, city and province.] See quality management.

items.q: Are field welds recorded the same way as shop welds?
items.a: Yes. The same qualified operators, procedures, coupons, log format and borescope records apply on site, and field welds are added to the weld maps and dossier before SAT.

items.q: Do we need electropolish?
items.a: Not by rule. SF1 mechanically polished is common for PW. We recommend SF4 electropolish for hot WFI, pure steam and tank interiors, where heat makes rouge more likely and a chromium-rich surface helps. Your URS or corporate standard decides; we state the finish on every component in the plan.

items.q: Is passivation done in-house?
items.a: [State whether shop passivation and electropolishing are done in-house or by a named subcontractor, and whether site passivation is done by Aquemi staff.] Either way the certificate names the standard, chemistry, temperature, contact time and verification test.

items.q: Who registers the pressure vessels?
items.a: Vessels are designed to ASME Section VIII, Division 1 and registered under CSA B51 with the authority in the province of installation, which issues the CRN. [State whether Aquemi holds an ASME certificate of authorization or uses a certified vessel fabricator, and the provinces where it has registered designs.] Fittings and, in some provinces, piping systems also need registration; we confirm what applies to your site at design.

items.q: Are the control panels certified?
items.a: [State the panel shop, whether panels carry a certification mark to CSA C22.2 No. 286 or UL 508A, and whether field evaluation is used otherwise.] An uncertified panel can be stopped at site by the electrical inspector, so we settle this before order.

items.q: Can we see a real weld log before we order?

pages.title: Water system FAT and SAT to EU GMP Annex 15 | Aquemi
pages.meta: Wet FAT on every skid to a protocol you approve, then SAT on your feed water. Written to EU GMP Annex 15, 3.6 so IQ and OQ can leverage results.
pages.eyebrow: FAT · SAT · EU GMP ANNEX 15 · GAMP 5 · ISPE BASELINE GUIDE VOL. 5
pages.headline: Watch your water system run wet, against a protocol you approved, before it leaves our test bay
pages.lead: Every skid runs in our test bay through a wet factory acceptance test (FAT): water in every line, every sequence, alarm, interlock and divert, a full sanitization cycle and outlet quality, to a protocol your quality unit approves before we start. EU GMP Annex 15, 3.6 lets tests performed at FAT stand without repeating them at installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) where transport and installation cannot affect them, so we write each test case to be leveraged. After tie-in, a site acceptance test (SAT) proves what only your site can: your feed water, your utilities and your network.
tags: ISPE Good Practice Guide: C&Q of water and steam

secondary_cta.label: Arrange a test bay visit or audit

blocks.h: A fault found in our test bay costs a day. Found on your site, it costs a shutdown window.
body: Most of what goes wrong at start-up is found by running water: a valve that opens in the wrong step, an interlock wired to the wrong input, a divert that never fires, a probe that never reaches 80 °C because it sits in a cold corner. In our shop the fix is a cable, a line of code or a fitting, made the same afternoon. On your site the same fix waits for a permit, a contractor and a slot between production campaigns.

So we test wet, not dry. A dry FAT checks wiring and screens. A wet FAT fills the skid, runs the pumps against real pressure, heats to sanitization temperature and measures conductivity and total organic carbon (TOC) at the outlet. Leaks, sequence errors and instrument faults show up while the skid is still on our floor.

And we write it once. Annex 15, 3.5 expects equipment to be confirmed against the user requirement specification (URS) and functional specification at the vendor, where applicable. GAMP 5 (second edition) and ASTM E2500 both tell the regulated company to leverage well-documented supplier testing rather than repeat it, and the ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 5 and the ISPE Good Practice Guide on commissioning and qualification (C&Q) of water and steam systems (third edition, 2025) apply that lifecycle to water systems. A FAT executed to an approved protocol, with calibrated instruments, raw data and signatures, is evidence your validation team can reference. A FAT run from a checklist is a demonstration, and gets repeated.

blocks.h: From protocol to release-to-ship

items.d: Written from the approved functional specification and the commissioning and qualification plan at detailed design, and sent [protocol issue before FAT, weeks] ahead, with an acceptance criterion and a URS or functional specification reference on every test case. See process design.

Your validation team comments; we answer each comment in writing and reissue. Annex 15, 2.6 asks your site to confirm a vendor protocol suits your procedures before approval, and allows you to add test cases. Nothing is executed before your quality unit signs.
We run the full protocol ourselves first and fix what it finds. The witnessed FAT should confirm the system, not debug it.
Your team on our floor or by video. Results recorded as found, in ink or electronically, with raw data printed or exported and attached. Fabrication hold points are already closed. See fabrication.

A failed acceptance criterion is a deviation: logged, investigated, fixed and retested. A defect that does not affect a test result goes on the punch list. Both are classified and assigned before the team leaves.
Executed protocol, deviation log, punch list and summary report signed by both parties. Release to ship with open items only on a documented assessment that they do not affect installation or SAT.

After mechanical completion, the SAT protocol re-runs the critical tests with your utilities and feed water, closes the punch list and hands the system to IQ and OQ. See commissioning and qualification.

blocks.h: What a FAT cannot prove, however well it is run
blocks.body: Our test bay runs on [test-bay feed water source and treatment], so outlet conductivity and TOC at FAT prove the skid can perform, not that it meets USP <645> and USP <643> on your water. Your feed water, its winter temperature, your utilities, your network and the field-built loop exist only on site. Microbial control is proven by sampling over time: performance qualification (PQ) is commonly run in three phases across about a year. FAT moves the functional risk off your site. It does not replace SAT, IQ, OQ or PQ.

blocks.h: Questions validation and quality teams ask

items.q: What does FAT prove if the skid runs on your test water, not our feed?
items.a: Function: every sequence, alarm, interlock and divert, a sanitization cycle reaching temperature at every probe, instrument loop checks, and outlet quality on our test water. Performance on your feed water is proven at SAT and OQ. We write the protocol so your quality unit can leverage FAT results under Annex 15, 3.6 and ASTM E2500, where it accepts that approach.

items.q: Will our quality unit accept FAT results in place of IQ/OQ tests?
items.a: That is its decision, and Annex 15 sets the test: appropriate, justified and unaffected by transport and installation. It helps when the leverage is planned, not argued afterwards. We mark candidate test cases in the commissioning and qualification plan at detailed design, your quality unit approves the FAT protocol before execution (Annex 15, 2.6), and the report shows calibrated instruments, raw data and signatures. Water quality on your feed and anything touching site utilities is never leveraged.

items.q: Can we use our own protocol template?
items.a: Yes. We write into your template and numbering, or deliver ours for you to adopt. Either way each test case carries a URS or functional specification reference, so it lands in your traceability matrix.

items.q: What can a remote witness not see?
items.a: Smell, noise and heat, the inside of a panel unless the camera is opened up to it, and the thread engagement of a fitting. For a remote FAT we agree in the protocol which checks need a person on site, and either send you close-up video and photos with the record or recommend a hybrid witness for those tests.

items.q: What if a test fails while you are watching?
items.a: It is recorded as found, as a deviation. We do not edit the acceptance criterion or quietly rerun the test; Annex 15, 2.7 treats a significant change to the approved protocol as a deviation too. We investigate, fix, and retest that case and any case the fix could affect, with you witnessing the retest.

items.q: Is the software we see at FAT the software that ships?
items.a: Yes. The programmable logic controller (PLC) and operator interface software is under version control, and its version and checksum are recorded in the protocol. Any change after FAT goes through change control with a stated regression test, and is shown again at SAT.

items.q: Do you FAT the distribution loop?
items.a: The loop pump and heat exchanger skid, the tank and the controls, yes. Loop piping is built on your site, so its slopes, branch lengths, welds and hydraulics are proven at SAT and IQ. See storage and distribution loops.

items.a: [State whether endotoxin sampling of still or membrane WFI output is offered at FAT and which laboratory tests it.] Like conductivity and TOC, it is a result on our feed water, so it supports, but does not replace, sampling on your site.

items.a: A packaged Purified Water skid takes [typical FAT duration, PW skid, days]; a generation and storage system takes [typical FAT duration, generation and storage, days]. Witness dates are set at order and confirmed [FAT date confirmation, weeks] ahead, after the dry run.

items.a: Yes. Test instruments are calibrated [calibration interval and traceability] and their certificates are bound into the executed FAT report, so your reviewer can check every reading against a calibrated instrument.

items.a: After FAT the skid is drained and [drying, capping and any gas blanket used]. Openings are sealed and tagged, its condition is recorded at dispatch and checked again on arrival, before SAT starts.

pages.title: Water system IQ, OQ and PQ to EU GMP Annex 15 | Aquemi
pages.meta: IQ and OQ to protocols your QA approves, then PQ in three phases over 12 months (WHO TRS 1033, FDA guide), with alert levels set from your own data.
pages.eyebrow: IQ · OQ · PQ · EU GMP ANNEX 15 · USP <1231> · WHO TRS 1033
pages.headline: A qualified water system your inspector can follow, from the first weld to a full year of data
pages.lead: We commission your water or pure steam system, execute installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) to protocols your quality unit approves, and run performance qualification (PQ) with you through the three phases a water system needs: two intensive phases of at least two weeks each, then routine monitoring until you hold at least 12 months of data across the seasons, as WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 and the FDA guide to high purity water systems describe. Your alert levels come out of that data, not out of a pharmacopoeia table.

secondary_cta.label: How FAT feeds IQ and OQ

blocks.h: Inspectors rarely fault the water. They fault the evidence behind it.
body: A water system can meet USP <645> and USP <643> every day and still produce an inspection finding. The usual causes are in the qualification file, not the pipework: an IQ that checked drawings nobody updated after the field welds, an OQ that never tested the coldest point of use during sanitization, a PQ started before the sanitization procedure was final, alert levels copied from the pharmacopoeia instead of derived from the system's own data, and a requalification that is either never done or repeated in full every year by habit.

Each of those is cheap to prevent and expensive to explain. So we plan qualification at detailed design, in a commissioning and qualification (C&Q) plan your quality unit approves, and we carry one set of requirement IDs from your user requirement specification (URS) through FAT, IQ, OQ and the PQ sampling plan. EU GMP Annex 15 (2015) sets the stages and who approves what; USP <1231>, the FDA Guide to Inspections of High Purity Water Systems and WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 (2021) set how a water system proves itself over time; the ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 5 and ASTM E2500 set how much of that you have to test twice.
Commissioning is part of it, but it is not the same thing. WHO TRS 1033, 11.2 puts it plainly: commissioning is documented, and it is not a replacement for qualification.

blocks.h: PQ in three phases
blocks.caption: Performance qualification phases · new water system
cols: Sampling, use of water and what the phase settles

rows.v: At least 2 weeks (WHO); the FDA guide describes 2 to 4 weeks
rows.m: Daily sampling of feed water, after each purification step, at every point of use and at the end of the loop. Sets operating ranges, sanitization and maintenance procedures, provisional alert and action levels and the test-failure procedure. Water is not used for manufacturing.

rows.v: At least a further 2 weeks
rows.m: Same sampling programme, now with every standard operating procedure (SOP) in use. Shows consistent operation within the established ranges. Water may be used for manufacturing during this phase if phase 1 and ongoing phase 2 data show the required quality and your QA approves it (WHO TRS 1033, 11.3).

rows.v: Until phases 1 to 3 cover at least 12 months
rows.m: Routine sampling plan, reduced from phase 1 and 2 data. For WFI the FDA guide describes a daily sample from at least one point of use with every point tested weekly. Data trended, for example quarterly, and the system reviewed at the end. Water is in use. Validation is complete when you hold a full year of data.

blocks.note: Phase content from WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 (2021), 11.3 and the FDA Guide to Inspections of High Purity Water Systems; USP <1231> and the ISPE Good Practice Guide on C&Q of water and steam systems take the same seasonal view, and EU GMP Annex 1, 6.8 asks that seasonal variation in feed water is considered. Durations, points and frequencies are fixed in your PQ protocol. For a change to an existing system, WHO allows the phases and their length to be set by documented risk assessment.

blocks.h: Sample size and method decide whether your PQ data mean anything
blocks.body: The FDA guide prefers 100 to 300 mL for WFI microbial samples and calls volumes under 100 mL unacceptable, because an action level of 10 colony-forming units (CFU) per 100 mL cannot be seen in 1 mL. It also asks that point-of-use samples reflect how water is drawn. We write sample volume, sanitized sample valve or hose, flush time, transport time and temperature, test method, medium and incubation into the sampling plan before phase 1 starts, and agree them with your microbiology laboratory, so phase 1 results are comparable with the year that follows.

blocks.h: Questions validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Do we really have to wait a year before using the water?
items.a: No. WHO TRS 1033 allows use during phase 2 when phase 1 and ongoing phase 2 data show the required quality and your QA approves it, and water is in use throughout phase 3. The year is how long it takes to complete validation, because it has to cover the seasonal changes in your feed water. Plan your first production batches against the end of phase 2, not the end of phase 3.

items.q: Can IQ and OQ be combined into one protocol?
items.a: Yes. Annex 15, 2.5 and 3.10 allow a combined installation and operational qualification (IOQ) where the system's complexity allows. On a packaged PW skid it often saves a review cycle; on a full generation, storage and pure steam system we usually keep them apart so IQ deviations do not hold up OQ testing of unaffected parts.

items.q: How much of IQ and OQ can FAT replace?
items.a: Documentation review and tests whose result transport and installation cannot change, where your quality unit accepts it (Annex 15, 3.6). We mark candidate tests in the C&Q plan and write the FAT protocol for your approval before execution. Water quality on your feed, site utilities and field-built piping are always proven on site. See FAT and SAT.

items.q: We work to ASTM E2500 verification, not IQ/OQ/PQ. Can you work that way?
items.a: Yes. The tests are much the same; what changes is the structure. Under ASTM E2500 and the ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 5, verification focuses on critical aspects found by risk assessment, subject matter experts carry more of the review, and your quality unit approves the acceptance and release. We write the C&Q plan in your model and keep the same traceability either way.

items.q: Who takes the PQ samples and who tests them?
items.a: Usually your operators and your laboratory, because the routine monitoring that follows is theirs too, and the method has to stay the same from phase 1 onward. We write or review the sampling plan, train your samplers, and [state whether Aquemi staff can take samples on site during phases 1 and 2, and through which laboratory].

items.q: What happens if an action level is exceeded during PQ?
items.a: It is a deviation under your procedure. We investigate with you: sampling technique, sample valve, the point's flush and use pattern, sanitization records and the trend at neighbouring points. The fix is verified with resampling, and if it changes a procedure or setpoint the phase may need to be extended. A PQ that shows an excursion found, explained and corrected is stronger evidence than one that shows none.

items.q: Why not use the pharmacopoeia limits as alert levels?
items.a: Because they tell you nothing until the water is already near failure. A loop that runs at 0.10 mg/L TOC and 2 CFU/100 mL needs warning long before 0.50 mg/L or 10 CFU/100 mL. Annex 1, 6.13 expects alert levels based on the system's qualification data. Microbial counts are rarely normally distributed, so a percentile of the PQ data often suits them better than a mean plus three standard deviations; your quality unit chooses the method.

items.q: Does pure steam need a three-phase PQ?
items.a: There is no pharmacopoeial three-phase rule for pure steam. We scope it by risk in the C&Q plan: condensate conductivity, TOC and endotoxin at each use point over an agreed period, and EN 285 non-condensable gas, dryness and superheat tests where the steam sterilizes, repeated periodically as Annex 1, 6.17 expects. See pure steam generators.

items.q: How often should we requalify?
items.a: Annex 15, 4.1 and 4.2 ask for evaluation at a justified frequency, not a full repeat. Most sites review the system annually, as WHO TRS 1033, 14.1 suggests, and requalify only what a change, a trend or the review points to. Repeating a full IQ/OQ every year by habit costs downtime and proves little.

items.q: Can you qualify or requalify a system you did not build?
items.a: Yes. We start with a gap assessment of the existing qualification file and the installed system against Annex 15, Annex 1 and your current requirements, then propose a scope your quality unit can approve. Missing as-built drawings, a dead leg register or calibration history are the usual gaps. See upgrades and requalification.

pages.eyebrow: SERVICE PLANS · CALIBRATION · SPARE PARTS · EU GMP ANNEX 15 · USP <645> · USP <643>
pages.headline: Service that keeps your water system running and keeps it qualified
pages.lead: Most water systems fall out of their qualified state on a maintenance day, not on a design drawing: a membrane of a different model, a calibration certificate nobody filed, a visit that never went through change control. Our service plans state the response time for each severity of fault, from [fastest on-site response, hours] for a critical fault, and fix the scope in writing. Every visit runs under your change control and maintenance procedures, calibrations meet USP <645> (cell constant known to ± 2 %) and USP <643> (system suitability 85–115 %), and the signed service report is written to go straight into your good manufacturing practice (GMP) records.

secondary_cta.label: Production stopped or water out of specification? Request urgent service

blocks.h: Your water passed PQ. Service decides whether it stays that way.
body: After performance qualification (PQ), the qualified state of a Purified Water (PW) or Water for Injection (WFI) system depends on what happens to it every month: which parts go in, who calibrates the instruments and against what, how a fault at 2 a.m. gets fixed, and whether the record of all of it survives an inspection. 21 CFR 211.67 and 211.68 require equipment to be maintained and instruments calibrated to a written programme, with records. EU GMP Chapter 3 asks that repair and maintenance present no hazard to product quality and that control equipment be calibrated at defined intervals. In Canada, section C.02.005 of the Food and Drug Regulations, as Health Canada interprets it in GUI-0001, expects the same.

So we sell service as a defined product, not a phone number. Each plan states its response times, visits, calibrations, spares and reports before you sign, and every task inside it is written to work with your procedures: work orders raised in your maintenance system, parts replaced like for like or routed through your change control under EU GMP Annex 15, section 11, and calibrations with certificates traceable to national standards. When something does change the system, we tell you which part of the requalification it touches. See commissioning and qualification for how that scope is set.

items.q: Will service work affect our qualified state?

We classify every part we replace in the report, and where something is not like for like we stop and give you the input for the change request, including the IQ, OQ or sampling we would propose. items.q: Can your technicians work to our SOPs and our forms?
items.a: Yes. If your procedures require your own work order, logbook or calibration forms, we complete those as well as or instead of ours. We send training records with the visit plan, take your site induction and GMP training where you require it, and follow your gowning and permit rules.

pages.title: Water system upgrades and retrofits, any builder | Aquemi
pages.meta: Upgrade a PW or WFI system from any builder: RO/EDI, sanitization, online TOC, Part 11 controls, dead legs, with the EU GMP Annex 15 requalification scope.
pages.eyebrow: UPGRADES · RETROFITS · ANY BUILDER · EU GMP ANNEX 15 · 21 CFR PART 11 · ASME BPE
pages.headline: Upgrade the water system you already have, with the requalification scope known before the first cut
pages.lead: Most upgrade projects that overrun do so in validation, not in fabrication: a controls swap that turns into a full software revalidation, a new branch that moves the coldest point of the loop, a route change nobody told the regulator about. We start with an assessment of your Purified Water (PW), Water for Injection (WFI) or pure steam system, whoever built it, and give you each option with its downtime and the installation, operational and performance qualification (IQ, OQ, PQ) it triggers under EU GMP Annex 15, section 11, before you raise the change request.

secondary_cta.label: Water out of specification or system down now? Request service

blocks.h: Your system is older than its controls and younger than the rules it is now judged by
body: A PW or WFI system installed fifteen years ago was qualified against the expectations of its day. Since then the revised EU GMP Annex 1 (2022, in force from August 2023 and adopted by Health Canada as GUI-0119) has asked for continuous total organic carbon (TOC) and conductivity monitoring on WFI systems, a sanitization schedule set from monitoring results and a contamination control strategy that covers water. Data integrity expectations under 21 CFR Part 11 and EU GMP Annex 11 have reached the controls cabinet. And the programmable logic controller (PLC) that runs the system may now be a part its maker no longer sells.

None of that forces a new system. It forces decisions, and each decision has two costs: the work itself and the requalification that follows it. Annex 15, section 11 asks that every planned change is assessed for its effect on the qualified state before it is made, and WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 allows the PQ phases and their length for a change to an existing system to be set by documented risk assessment rather than repeated in full. Used well, that saves months. Used badly, it produces either a short PQ an inspector questions or a full year of sampling nobody needed.

So we price the requalification with the work. Every option in an assessment report states what changes physically, which documents and tests it touches, how long the water is unavailable, and how you keep supplying production while it is done.

blocks.h: Common upgrades, and the requalification scope to plan for each

rows.t: Chemical deionization (DI) to reverse osmosis (RO) and electrodeionization (EDI)

rows: Remove acid and caustic regeneration or exchange-tank deliveries, get steadier conductivity, and take resin beds that stand at ambient temperature out of the generation step
New generation skid, pretreatment matched to RO (chlorine removal, softening, antiscalant), new drain and reject routing; the loop usually stays

IQ and OQ of the new generation skid, leveraging factory acceptance tests (FAT) where your quality unit accepts them. Intensive sampling after each step, at the loop return and at points of use for a risk-assessed period, then a reduced plan; alert levels reviewed on the new data
Annex 15, section 11; WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3, 11.3

rows.t: Hot water sanitization on an ambient loop

rows: Replace chemical sanitization, or meet Annex 1, 6.12 with a schedule your data support

Loop heater on a sanitary double tube sheet heat exchanger, temperature probes at the coldest points, heated vent filter, allowance for expansion; every component checked for its rating at the sanitization temperature

IQ of the new equipment and of material and pressure ratings. OQ of the full cycle with temperature recorded at the coldest probe for the hold time, then sampling long enough to show control at the new frequency
USP <1231> (65–80 °C commonly used); Annex 1, 6.12

rows.t: Ozone and destruct UV on an ambient loop

rows: Sanitize PW or membrane WFI loops without heat cycles, or loops whose piping is not rated for heat

Ozone generator and injection at the tank, 254 nm ultraviolet (UV) destruct before the loop supply, dissolved ozone sensors in the tank, after the UV and on the return, ozone-compatible seals and diaphragms, a room gas monitor and a safe vent route

IQ, including an elastomer compatibility review. OQ of the tank ozone set point, of ozone absent after the UV and at points of use before release, and of the loop sanitization with the UV off. Intensive microbial sampling through the first sanitization intervals
ISPE Baseline Guide Vol. 4 (0.02–0.2 ppm); Annex 1, 6.12

rows.t: Online TOC and conductivity, or real-time release

Computerized system validation under GAMP 5: specifications, risk assessment, software FAT on a simulator, IQ of hardware and software, OQ of every sequence, alarm and interlock, data integrity tests, and migration or retention of legacy records. Short water sampling after cutover where the process itself is unchanged

Full replacement
A system beyond economic repair, or several of the upgrades above at once

As a new system: FAT, commissioning, IQ, OQ and a three-phase PQ to at least 12 months, with cutover planned so the old system supplies production until release

blocks.h: We size requalification by what the change can affect, not by habit
blocks.body: For each option we list the critical aspects the change can reach: water quality at generation, in the loop and at the points of use, the sanitization cycle, and the data your release depends on. Anything outside that reach is left alone, and the reasoning goes into the change impact assessment so your quality unit can sign it and an inspector can follow it. Where the risk assessment is borderline, we say so and propose the longer sampling period.

blocks.h: Systems whose builder has changed hands
body: Many PW and WFI systems in service in North America were built by companies that have since been sold, merged or renamed. Evoqua became part of Xylem in 2023, a year after buying the renal business that Mar Cor and Cantel had operated under STERIS. Grundfos agreed to acquire MECO in 2021 and completed its acquisition of Newterra in 2025. Ecolab bought Ovivo's electronics ultrapure water business in 2025. Systems keep running through changes like these. What tends to change is who answers the phone, which part numbers are current, and who still holds the software.

We work on systems we did not build. [Confirm the equipment types and makes Aquemi services and upgrades.] The first step is the same as for our own: an assessment of the system as it stands and of the records behind it, so that every later replacement is checked like for like against a known original, and every upgrade starts from a drawing that matches the pipework.

body: EDI module makers present continuous electrodeionization as a chemical-free alternative to mixed-bed DI with lower operating and maintenance cost. Whether that holds for your plant depends on your water volume, your exchange-tank or chemical cost, your drain charges and your power cost, so the assessment works the comparison out per cubic metre of water for your system rather than quoting a percentage. blocks.h: Obsolete controllers: replace them before the last spare is used
body: Several controller families common on water systems are discontinued or in phase-out, for example Allen-Bradley PLC-5 and SLC 500 and Siemens S5 and S7-300. Replacing the controller is never like for like: even a converted program is new software under Annex 11 and GAMP 5, and every sequence, alarm and interlock is tested again. We build the new panel and test the program against a simulator at our shop, so site work is the swap, the IQ and the OQ, in a window of [controls swap window, days]. Monitoring and controls describes the validated architecture we replace them with.

blocks.h: Changing the WFI route
body: Since 1 April 2017, Ph. Eur. 0169 accepts WFI made by reverse osmosis coupled with other suitable techniques, and USP has long allowed any process equivalent or superior to distillation. A move from a still to membrane WFI saves plant steam and cooling water, but it replaces one phase change with several barriers in series and a documented control strategy, as the EMA questions and answers on non-distillation WFI (EMA/INS/GMP/443117/2017) expect. For Ph. Eur. markets it also needs notice to your GMP supervisory authority before implementation.

The move can run the other way. A site that needs hot WFI for a hot loop, or that supplies a market or works to a corporate standard that still calls for distillation, may replace a membrane skid with a still. In both directions we build the new generator alongside the old one where space allows, so the existing system supplies production until your quality unit releases the new water, and the route assessment checks every market you release into. Ask your regulatory team whether your marketing authorizations or site master file describe the WFI route; if they do, the change may need a filing as well as change control.

blocks.h: Questions engineering, validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Our system was built by another supplier. Will you work on it?
items.a: [Confirm scope.] Yes, starting with an assessment. We need whatever records you have. Where drawings, the PLC program or the qualification file are missing, the assessment report lists what to recover and what it costs to recreate it, before any upgrade is designed.

items.q: Will an upgrade restart our PQ from zero?
items.a: Not usually. WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 allows the PQ phases and their length after a change to an existing system to be set by documented risk assessment. A new generation step or a route change justifies an intensive phase; a new branch justifies sampling at that branch and its neighbours; a controller swap with the process unchanged may justify only short sampling after cutover. Your quality unit decides; we write the rationale it needs.

items.q: Can we keep producing water during the upgrade?
items.a: Usually. Most generation upgrades are built alongside the running system and tied in during a short shutdown. Loop work needs a planned shutdown, followed by sanitization and sampling before release, so we plan it against your production schedule and your storage volume. Where the shutdown is longer than storage can cover, the options say so.

items.q: Is a PLC replacement really a full revalidation?
items.a: Of the control system, yes, because the software is new even when the logic is converted. Of the water system, no: if sequences, set points and equipment are unchanged, the process qualification stands and the water sampling after cutover is short. Testing the software against a simulator before site work keeps the on-site part of that validation short.

items.q: We cannot get the PLC program or passwords from the original supplier.
items.a: Then a modification cannot be validated, and we plan a replacement. We document the running system first, from its inputs and outputs, observed sequences, set points and alarms and your functional requirements, so the new program is specified from evidence rather than memory.

items.q: Does adding ozone or hot water sanitization change our microbial limits?
items.a: No. Limits come from the pharmacopoeia and your specification. What changes is how the system holds them, so the OQ proves the new cycle at the coldest or most remote point, and the sampling period afterwards shows the new frequency works. Alert levels are then reviewed on the new data.

items.q: Do we need to tell a regulator about the change?
items.a: For most upgrades, change control is enough. The exceptions to check are a move to membrane WFI, where Ph. Eur. 0169 asks for notice to your GMP supervisory authority before implementation, and any change to something your marketing authorization or site master file describes. Your regulatory team decides; we supply the technical documents behind it.

items.q: We make more than one kind of product. Which page do we read?

A plant making oral solids and one sterile line reads the sterile rows of the pharmaceutical page; a device maker with a drug-device combination product also reads the pharmaceutical page for the drug part. items.q: Do the limits change with the industry?
items.a: No. USP <645>, <643> and <85>, and the Ph. Eur. monographs, set the same limits for PW and WFI whoever uses them. What changes is which grade each step needs, the device limits a device maker works back from, and how the record is audited. Microbial alert and action levels are yours to set; USP <1231> gives guidance of 100 CFU/mL for PW and 10 CFU/100 mL for WFI.

blocks.h: The water system is the first utility an inspector walks
body: Water is the excipient most drug products use most, the final rinse of almost every cleaning cycle and the feed to every WFI still and pure steam generator. An inspection of a water system reads the design, the qualification and the trend data together: slopes and dead legs on the drawings, the sanitization record, the alert and action levels and what was done when one was crossed.

Most of the water findings we are asked to fix were set at design: a loop with no spare capacity for the next product line, a point of use added without a drawing update, a qualification file with no weld records, an endotoxin target for a WFI still that nobody wrote down. We start from your products, your markets and your expansion plan, then choose the systems and write the records that answer those questions before an inspector asks them.

We work for innovator and generic drug manufacturers, natural health product (NHP) makers and contract manufacturers in Canada, on oral solid dose (OSD), non-sterile liquid and semi-solid, and sterile and parenteral lines.

blocks.h: How the systems connect in a pharmaceutical plant
blocks.caption: An oral solid dose or liquids plant usually stops at the PW loop. A sterile plant also feeds PW to a WFI still or membrane WFI skid and to a pure steam generator, which serves autoclaves and SIP directly. So the PW system is sized for its own points of use plus that feed demand, and designed to the still's and generator's feed limits. Pretreatment keeps chlorine, chloramine and scale off the membranes through Canadian winter and summer feed water. Monitoring and controls run across all of it, with audit-trailed records under 21 CFR Part 11 and EU GMP Annex 11.

items.d: A generics site that adds a liquid line or a sterile suite needs more PW, or a WFI feed, from the same generator. We size headers and generator capacity for the plan you can see and write the expansion into the user requirement specification (URS).
USP stage 1 conductivity is the tighter value for PW; Ph. Eur. adds nitrates and its own microbial method. Designing to both costs little at the start and a lot to add after qualification.

Both routes are pharmacopoeial in USP and Ph. Eur. Distillation fills a hot loop and has the longer record with inspectors. Membrane WFI uses less energy and needs a stronger control strategy and, for EU markets, a notice to the supervisory authority.

Hot circulation above 70 °C is the example Annex 1 gives for WFI. PW loops are often ambient with periodic hot water or ozone sanitization. The choice sets energy use, point-of-use cooling and the sanitization record you keep.

Feed temperature can swing from near freezing in winter to over 20 °C in summer, and some municipal supplies use chloramine. We size membranes at your coldest month and design chloramine removal and carbon dioxide control together.

Duplex generation trains and isolable loop sections let you sanitize, service or tie in new points of use without stopping every line. We plan tie-ins around your shutdown calendar and change control.

items.q: Do we need WFI if all our products are non-sterile?
items.a: Usually not. The EMA guideline sets PW as the minimum for oral, cutaneous, nasal, ear, rectal and vaginal products and for granulation and coating. The exceptions are products that must be sterile and non-pyrogenic, such as some nebuliser solutions. Your product registration and specification decide.

items.q: Can one system supply products for Canada, the United States and Europe?
items.a: Yes. We design to the stricter of USP and Ph. Eur. on each attribute, test both at FAT where the methods allow it, and write both into the functional specification, so the same records answer Health Canada, the FDA and an EU importer.

items.q: Is membrane WFI acceptable to Health Canada and the FDA?
items.a: USP allows WFI by distillation or a purification process shown to be equivalent or superior to it, and Ph. Eur. 0169 has allowed reverse osmosis with other techniques since April 2017. Health Canada applies the pharmacopoeia named in your product file. For EU markets, notice goes to the GMP supervisory authority before use. Confirm the route with your regulatory team product by product; the WFI by membrane page sets out the control strategy.

items.q: We make natural health products. Do we need USP Purified Water?
items.a: GUI-0158 sets potable water as the minimum. A PW skid on the same platform as a drug-grade system can be qualified to the level your product needs.

items.q: We are adding a production line. Must the whole water system be requalified?
items.a: Not normally. The change goes through your change control, and a risk assessment sets the qualification scope: usually IQ and OQ for the new section and a period of increased sampling at the new points of use. We state that scope before the first cut and plan the tie-in around your shutdown.

items.q: Can we use the water during PQ?
items.a: WHO TRS 1033 Annex 3 allows use in phase 2 of PQ with quality unit approval, after a first phase of at least two weeks with no manufacturing use. Your validation master plan decides. The commissioning and qualification page sets out each phase.

pages.headline: WFI for biologics that holds endotoxin at every point of use, from the clinical suite to the commercial plant
pages.lead: A biologics plant draws Water for Injection (WFI) in volume for media, buffers and the final rinse of every clean-in-place (CIP) cycle, and pure steam for sterilize-in-place (SIP) and autoclaves. Endotoxin in that water ends up in your process, so we design the loop to hold the USP <85> limit of < 0.25 EU/mL, USP <645> 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C and 500 ppb total organic carbon (TOC) at the furthest outlet, at peak draw. We size it for your batch schedule, leave room for the next suite, and hand over the factory acceptance test (FAT) report and installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) protocols that Health Canada, the FDA and EU inspectors read.

blocks.h: In a biologics plant, water is a process input, not a utility in the background
body: Cell culture media, chromatography and filtration buffers, CIP rinses and the feed to every pure steam generator all start as WFI or Purified Water (PW). Buffer and media preparation draw large volumes in short windows and then stop, so peak draw, not daily total, sets the storage tank, the pump and the loop.

Endotoxin is a critical quality attribute in almost every biologic drug substance and drug product specification. It is heat stable: sanitization kills the bacteria that shed it, but does not destroy what they have already released. A biofilm in a cooled sub-loop or a point-of-use exchanger can put endotoxin into a full media batch long before a monthly sample shows it. We design those weak spots out and show the evidence at qualification.

We work for biologics developers and contract manufacturers, vaccine makers, and cell and gene therapy facilities in Canada, including university and hospital buildings that make advanced therapy medicinal products (ATMPs) for clinical trials.

items.q: We are a start-up with one clinical product. Is a full WFI system justified?

pages.headline: Final rinse water you can defend in your cleaning validation and at your next MDSAP audit
pages.lead: For most devices the last thing to touch the product before packaging is water. Endotoxin and bioburden left by that rinse count against the device: USP <161> sets 20.0 EU per device, and 2.15 EU per device for cerebrospinal fluid contact, and the bioburden you measure to ISO 11737-1 sets your sterilization dose. We design Purified Water (PW) and Water for Injection (WFI) systems that hold USP <645> 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C, 500 ppb total organic carbon (TOC) and the endotoxin and microbial limits your risk assessment sets, at the washer inlet, and we hand over factory acceptance test (FAT) and installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) records that fit an ISO 13485 quality system.
pages.primary_cta: Request a device water scope review

blocks.h: In a device plant, rinse water is part of a validated process
body: No standard sets one water grade for medical device manufacturing. ISO 13485:2016 asks you to control product cleanliness (7.5.2) and contamination (6.4.2), to validate any process whose output you cannot fully verify (7.5.6), and to maintain the infrastructure behind it (6.3). Cleaning is such a process, so the water at the end of it is part of your validation, and a water excursion is a cleaning deviation.

Three things set the grade: what the device contacts, how it is sterilized, and the release limits on the finished device. A non-sterile device for intact skin can be rinsed in PW. An implant, a blood-contacting device or anything for the central nervous system is usually rinsed in water with a written endotoxin limit, because endotoxin is heat stable and survives every common sterilization method. A device sterilized by radiation or ethylene oxide (EO) carries the bioburden its last rinse left, and that bioburden sets the dose.

Since 2 February 2026 the FDA Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR, 21 CFR 820) incorporates ISO 13485:2016 by reference. Health Canada licenses Class II to IV devices on an ISO 13485 certificate issued under the Medical Device Single Audit Program (MDSAP). One set of water system records can now answer both.

blocks.h: How the systems connect in a device plant
blocks.caption: Reverse osmosis (RO) with electrodeionization (EDI) makes PW, stored and circulated in an ambient loop under ozone or UV control, or hot where the demand profile suits it. Final rinse points for implants and blood-contact devices take water through ultrafiltration or from a membrane WFI skid; general rinses and passivation lines take PW from the loop. A clean steam generator fed with PW serves in-house steam sterilizers. Monitoring and controls run across all of it, with audit-trailed records under 21 CFR Part 11.

items.t: An endotoxin limit on PW, or WFI
items.d: Many device makers rinse in PW held to a written endotoxin limit, polished by ultrafiltration at the point of use. WFI is simpler to defend for CSF-contact devices. We work the rinse water limit back from your device limit and extraction volume, then compare both routes.
Water quality at the generator is not the water on your device. We put the specification and the sample point at the washer inlet, where your cleaning validation needs it.

items.t: Washer fill profile, not daily total
items.d: Washers and ultrasonic baths fill fast and then stop. Storage, pump and loop are sized from how many fill at once, how much and how fast.

Ambient loops with ozone suit most device plants and use less energy; they need ozone removal proven before use. A hot loop suits plants that also need WFI or rinse hot. We compare them on your demand.

items.t: A rinse endpoint you can measure
items.d: A final rinse validated to a conductivity or TOC endpoint at the washer drain gives you a release check on every cycle, not only during validation.

Feed temperature can swing from near freezing in winter to over 20 °C in summer, and some municipal supplies use chloramine. We size membranes at your coldest month and design chloramine removal ahead of the RO.

blocks.h: Adjacent use: water for hospital device reprocessing (MDRD)
body: Hospitals that reprocess reusable devices in a medical device reprocessing department (MDRD), or sterile processing department, work to different rules from device makers. In Canada that is CSA Z314, Canadian medical device reprocessing; in the United States, ANSI/AAMI ST108:2023, Water for the processing of medical devices, which replaced AAMI TIR34. ST108 sets categories for utility water, critical water for final rinse and steam generation, and steam. There is no ISO 13485 product release behind it, but the risk is the same: water left on an instrument goes into a patient.

The same RO and EDI platform we build for device makers can be built for hospital reprocessing water under CSA Z314, usually with duplex or N+1 redundancy because an MDRD cannot stop. [State Aquemi's scope for hospital MDRD and sterile processing water: new systems, upgrades of existing systems, service only, or not offered; and whether Aquemi bids hospital and health authority tenders.] If you run an MDRD, send the standard you work to with a scope review request and we will say plainly what we can supply.

blocks.h: Questions device engineering, validation and QA leads ask

items.q: Do we need WFI for our final rinse?
items.a: Only if your risk assessment says the rinse water must meet the WFI endotoxin limit, which is common for devices that contact cerebrospinal fluid. For most implants and blood-contact devices, PW with a written endotoxin limit and point-of-use ultrafiltration does the job at lower cost. We show the calculation from your device limit either way.

items.q: Our rinse water meets USP Purified Water. Is that enough for implant cleaning validation?
items.a: Not on its own. The USP PW monograph sets conductivity and TOC but no endotoxin limit, and its microbial level is guidance in USP <1231>, not a monograph limit. If endotoxin or bioburden on the device matters, write those limits into the water specification and sample at the washer inlet.

items.q: How does rinse water affect our radiation sterilization dose?
items.a: Your dose is set and audited from device bioburden measured to ISO 11737-1. A rise in rinse water bioburden shows up as higher device bioburden and can fail a dose audit under ISO 11137-2. Stable, trended rinse water is one of the cheapest ways to protect a validated dose.

items.q: What changed for our water system under the QMSR?
items.a: The FDA requirements now read as ISO 13485:2016 clauses: infrastructure, contamination control, process validation, calibration. If your water system already sits in an ISO 13485 system, the records are largely the same. We map our documents to those clauses so one package serves MDSAP, Health Canada and the FDA.

items.q: Is the water system validated or qualified?
items.a: Both words get used. Under ISO 13485 7.5.6 the cleaning process is validated; the water system that supplies it is qualified by IQ and OQ, with PQ evidence from routine sampling. We follow GHTF SG3/N99-10, the process validation guidance most device auditors know.

pages.lead: A contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) does not get one water audit a year. It gets one per client, plus Health Canada, the FDA and EU or other PIC/S inspectors for the markets those clients sell into, and an outage stops several clients' batches at once. We design Purified Water (PW) and Water for Injection (WFI) systems to the stricter of USP and Ph. Eur. on each attribute: USP <645> 1.3 µS/cm at 25 °C, Ph. Eur. nitrates 0.2 ppm, 500 ppb total organic carbon (TOC) and, for WFI, < 0.25 EU/mL endotoxin at the point of use. We build in the redundancy your client commitments need, and hand over the factory acceptance test (FAT) report, installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) records and trend data under 21 CFR Part 11 that any client auditor can follow without a guide.

blocks.h: In a CDMO, the water system is shared evidence
body: Every product on your site is made with the same water, so every client's quality unit reads the same records. One client audits against its US filing, the next against Ph. Eur. and its EU Qualified Person's checklist, a third sends a supplier questionnaire before it signs. Health Canada inspects the site under your drug establishment licence, and the FDA and EU or other PIC/S authorities inspect it when a client's product is filed in their market.

That changes what a good water system is. It has to meet the strictest market any client ships to, on every attribute, before the client asks. Its records have to be portable: a trend report, an excursion history or a change log you can send to one client without showing another client's data. It has to absorb a new programme on a tech transfer timeline you did not set. And it has to keep running, because a day without water is a day of missed batches across several contracts.

Your water system is also part of your sales pitch. When a prospective client's due diligence team asks what water you make, how you trend it and what happens when it fails, a clear answer helps win the programme. We design for that question from the user requirement specification (URS).

pages.lead: Your auditor will ask which standard each design decision answers to, and where the record is. This page lists every standard our system, service and industry pages cite for Purified Water (PW), Water for Injection (WFI) and pure steam: what it governs, the number we design to, the page that shows how, and the document in your turnover package that proves it. Limits are written as the standards state them, from USP <645> conductivity to Canadian registration numbers (CRN) under CSA B51 for pressure equipment. blocks.h: A standard is a design input, not a certificate
body: USP and Ph. Eur. set limits for water. They do not approve equipment, and no water system is "USP certified". What your inspector accepts is water that meets the monograph at your points of use, measured on qualified instruments, and a record that traces each requirement to a test. We design to the standards below, prove function at the factory acceptance test (FAT), prove performance on your feed water at the site acceptance test (SAT) and operational qualification (OQ), and support your performance qualification (PQ).

The tables are the list we start from. Your URS adds the pharmacopoeias your markets release to, your corporate engineering standard and your province of installation. We write the final list, with editions, into the functional specification so your validation team and ours work from one reference. Where USP and Ph. Eur. differ, we design to the stricter value on each attribute.

blocks.h: Questions validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Is your system USP certified?
items.a: No water system is. USP and Ph. Eur. set limits for water, not approvals for equipment. Compliance is shown by water at your points of use that meets the monograph, measured on qualified instruments, and by the records behind it. We design to the limits, prove function at FAT and performance on your feed water at SAT and OQ, and hand over the evidence listed on this page.

items.q: Do you design to USP or Ph. Eur.?
items.a: To the stricter value on each attribute when your products ship to both: USP <645> stage 1 for PW conductivity, Ph. Eur. 0008 for nitrates, 0.50 mg/L TOC validated for both. The functional specification names the monographs and editions that apply. The contract manufacturing page sets out each attribute side by side.

items.q: Which edition of each standard do you design to?
items.a: The edition in force when you approve the functional specification, named there. When a text changes during a project, as Ph. Eur. 0008 did in Ph. Eur. 12.3 from 1 July 2026, we assess the change under change control and tell you whether it touches the design, the tests or neither.

items.q: Is your control system 21 CFR Part 11 compliant?
items.a: No system is compliant on its own; your site is, by technical controls in the system plus procedures. We supply the technical controls (audit trail, access control, electronic signatures, record protection and backups) and a written Part 11 and Annex 11 assessment your quality unit can review.

items.q: Who registers our pressure equipment, and when?
items.a: Pressure vessels and fittings installed in Canada need a CRN under CSA B51 from the province of installation. We include registration in the project schedule from the start, because a design built for another market may need changes before it is accepted. [Confirm Aquemi's CRN process and the provinces covered.]

items.q: We have our own corporate engineering standard. Does it replace yours?
items.a: It adds to this list. Send it with the URS: we add it to the standards list in the functional specification and flag any clause that conflicts with a standard here, so your team decides before detailed design, not at IQ.

items.q: Will you complete our supplier questionnaire or quality agreement?

blocks.h: The package is the record your inspector reads
body: An inspector does not test your water system. They read its record: why each design decision was made, what each part is made of, how each weld was inspected and which test proved each requirement. At IQ your team checks the installation against that record, line by line (EU GMP Annex 15, 3.9). When a document is missing or late, IQ waits for it, and so does your release.

So we write the package as we go. Each document is issued at the stage that produces it, goes to your team for review while the work is still open, and lands in one turnover package indexed to your URS. The index below is the full list: every document our system and service pages promise, what it proves, when you see it, its format and who approves it. Your proposal lists the subset that applies to your system.

blocks.h: Questions validation and quality teams ask

items.q: Can we see real documents before we order?
items.a: Yes, redacted. The sample turnover package above shows the index, protocol contents and record formats from a delivered system, with customer names and data removed. [Confirm which samples are shared openly and which under NDA.] Your QA team can also audit how the records are produced: [what an audit covers, for example the fabrication shop and document control].

items.q: When do we see the protocols?
items.a: The FAT protocol reaches your quality unit [protocol issue before FAT, weeks] before testing, for approval before execution (EU GMP Annex 15, 2.6). IQ and OQ protocols follow the FAT, so they can reference its results rather than repeat them.

items.q: Can FAT results count towards qualification?
items.a: Where your quality unit agrees, yes. EU GMP Annex 15, 3.6 lets FAT tests stand where transport and installation cannot affect them, and the ISPE approach leverages engineering tests carried out under good documentation practice. We mark candidate test cases in the C&Q plan at detailed design, so the leverage is planned, not argued afterwards. Water quality on your feed is never leveraged.

items.q: Do you check third-party certificates, or just forward them?
items.a: We check them. At receipt, material markings are checked against the certificate [PMI, standard or option], and the material log ties each product-contact component to its EN 10204 3.1 certificate by heat number. Certificates are delivered as the issuer sent them, never retyped, so your reviewer sees the original.

This page shows how our quality management system (QMS) works, process by process: document control, change control, nonconformance and corrective and preventive action (CAPA), supplier control, calibration, training and internal audit, each with the record it leaves. blocks.h: A supplier audit tests whether records are made by a system or by memory
body: An auditor qualifying a water system supplier does not stop at the quality manual. They pick a weld, a certificate or a change and ask to see how it was controlled: who approved the drawing revision, which instrument took the reading and when it was last calibrated, what happened to the weld that failed borescope. If the answer is a person remembering, the finding is the supplier's, and the risk becomes yours at installation qualification (IQ).

So our QMS is written as procedures that each produce a record, and the records are the ones that land in your turnover package. [ISO 9001 status: certified by [registrar], certificate [number], scope [scope], expiry [date]; or: QMS built to the clauses of ISO 9001:2015, certification targeted for [date].] The tables below name the ISO 9001:2015 clause each process answers so your auditor can map it to your own supplier checklist. Where your quality agreement or user requirement specification (URS) asks for more, it governs and is written into the project quality plan.

blocks.h: Change control: what happens when something changes after you approve it

items.d: Anyone can raise a change request: a different valve, a revised setpoint, a routing change, a substitute material. It names the documents it touches, at their current revision.
Engineering and quality assess the impact on water quality, the critical aspects and critical design elements, the drawings, the functional specification and any test already executed.
A change to a document your team approved goes to your team before it is made. Internal-only changes are approved by Aquemi quality. Nothing is built to an unapproved revision.
Documents reissued at the next revision, superseded copies withdrawn from the shop and site, and the shop briefed.
The test that proves the change is run or repeated, for example a FAT test case, a software version and checksum record, or a pressure test after a piping change.

Closed in the change control register, which travels with the turnover package. After handover, changes you request run through your change control, with our impact assessment input (EU GMP Annex 15, section 11).

blocks.h: Nonconformance and CAPA: how a defect is found, held and closed
rows: Identify and hold

The item is tagged and segregated, or the work stopped, so it cannot move to the next step by mistake. Examples: a heat that does not match its certificate, a weld that fails borescope, a test result outside its acceptance criterion
Whoever finds it
NCR raised, with a number, the item and the requirement it fails
Disposition
Reject and replace, rework to the original requirement, or accept as is. A rejected product-contact weld is cut out, not ground or re-fused, and the replacement gets a new weld number
Aquemi quality. Accept as is, or any repair that departs from an approved document, needs your approval

For repeat, systemic or client-reported nonconformances, the cause is investigated, not just the item fixed
